Stand-In Effects and Pooling Amplification: Design-Based Tests of Whether Biological World Models Use Actions

Bowen Xu∗⁣†*\dagger bxu666@stanford.edu
Department of Biology, Stanford University, Stanford, CA, USA
Boyu Chen∗*
Institute of Health Informatics, University College London, London, UK
∗*Equal contribution. †\daggerCorresponding author.
Abstract

Action-conditioned world models are increasingly trained on data from randomized experiments, and whether their predictions respond to actions is usually checked by replacing or removing the actions and measuring the loss in accuracy. We show that such diagnostics report action effects where there are none: under autocorrelated designs, future actions stand in for history the model does not see, and a better model learns the stand-in better. When the design law is known, a conditional randomization test written as an e-value is valid in finite samples whatever the model, provided the resampler conditions on the full state the design used; resampling from a simpler law reproduces the false effect. We identify a second failure, specific to world models: when many sites share one action sequence—cells in a microscope field, pixels in a frame—the natural pooled score turns small model errors along the action contrast into overwhelming evidence against a true effect. In a pixel world, its median log e-value fell from −-17.3 to −-6832 as frames grew from 6464 to 40964096 pixels, while the oracle’s rose. Tempering the score by a design effect estimated on training data changes the bet, not the validity. Our own preregistered analysis of optogenetic ERK experiments failed in exactly this way; a tempered statistic, selected on synthetic data and registered before the data were obtained, then rejected the null on a never-opened field (E≈1.1×1010E\approx 1.1\times 10^{10}). Every analysis is preregistered, fixed in a dated protocol before it was run, or labelled exploratory, and every reported result is generated from hashed result files.

1 Introduction

World models that predict how a system will evolve under a sequence of actions are now trained on data from experiments as well as from simulators. In biology the actions are often stimulation programs—light pulses delivered to optogenetically engineered cells, for example—and the hope is that a model trained on such data will answer interventional questions: what would this cell population do under a different program? Before such a model is trusted for that purpose, one wants to know whether its action channel reflects a causal effect of the actions at all. In machine learning this is usually checked with diagnostics that replace the actions by zeros, by another unit’s actions or by a shuffled sequence, or retrain the model without them, and report an effect if predictions get worse. Recent benchmarks for action following in world models instead compare generated rollouts with simulator replays of expert and off-expert actions (Chen et al., 2026; Co et al., 2026), or score rollouts under perturbed or commanded actions with trajectory estimators, vision-language judges or human annotation (Yang et al., 2026a; Yang et al., 2026b); Oefinger et al. (2026) propose a ladder of checks that a world-model simulator must pass before its verdicts are trusted. None of them reports a test with finite-sample error control. Neither route is available, or reliable, when the data come from a real experiment that cannot be replayed.

The stand-in trap.

Replacement diagnostics fail in a simple way. Experimental designs are often autocorrelated: the next stimulus depends on the stimuli before it. A model that sees only a window of recent history can then use the future actions as a stand-in for earlier history that still drives the outcome. Its predictions change when the future actions change, so every replacement diagnostic reports an effect, even when the actions have none; and a model that predicts better learns the stand-in better (Proposition 6). In development simulations the replacement diagnostics reported effects in up to 249/256 replicates of such a null with twelve units, and in 256/256 for every model with 512512 units; in a pixel world in which the logging policy depends on state the model cannot see they did so in 64.1% to 100% of test episodes (§7, Figure 4).

A design-based test.

When actions were assigned by a randomized program whose law is known, that law supplies exactly what the diagnostics lack. Drawing alternative action blocks from the design law, given everything the design conditioned on, yields blocks that carry the same stand-in information as the observed one; under the null of no effect within the horizon the observed block is exchangeable with them. Scoring the observed and the resampled blocks with the world model gives a conditional randomization test (Candès et al., 2018) in which the model is only a statistic: it determines power, never validity. Written as an e-value, the test can be multiplied over time and across units and averaged across models without any assumption on the model or on shared noise (§3, Proposition 1). The conditioning matters: in a post hoc analysis, a resampler that draws each action from its marginal frequency rejected the same pixel-world null in 98.4% to 100% of episodes, while the design-law resampler rejected in none for the two-model average (§7.2).

Pooling amplification.

World models raise a second difficulty that does not arise for a single outcome. In an ERK optogenetics experiment, each microscope field receives one light program and records hundreds of cells; in a pixel world, every pixel of a frame shares the frame’s actions. The natural statistic sums the sites’ log predictive densities and bets on the result. If the model errs along the action contrast in a way the sites share, the sum multiplies that error by the number of sites, and the e-value is driven toward zero however strong the true effect is (§3.3). We met this failure in our own registered analysis: on the ERK positive controls, where light is known to drive the reporter, the pooled statistic gave log⁡E=−9576\log E=-9576 (§8.2). In the pixel world, its median log⁡E\log E fell from −-17.3 to −-6832 as frames grew from 6464 to 40964096 pixels, while the oracle’s rose from 79.0 to 157 (§6, Figure 1).

A repair that cannot break validity.

Because the design, not the statistic, controls the error rate, the pooled score may be tempered by any factor fixed on training data. We temper by an inverse design effect: the statistic registered for our confirmatory test uses the Kish factor of the residual correlation, and an exploratory variant measures the design effect along the action contrast, which is what governs amplification (§3.4). The Kish-tempered statistic, selected on synthetic data, gave log⁡E=349\log E=349 on the same ERK test fields in an exploratory reanalysis, and in a confirmatory test registered before the data were obtained it rejected the null on an ERK field that no one involved had opened, with E≈1.1×1010E\approx 1.1\times 10^{10} (§8.4). In the pixel world, where the Kish factor does not capture the relevant correlation, contrast tempering restored power under every noise condition we simulated, at the larger of the two effect sizes.

Contributions.

  1. 1.

    We describe the stand-in trap for action diagnostics of learned world models, give a construction in which replacement diagnostics detect a nonexistent effect with probability tending to one (Proposition 6), and show that a design-based test avoids it only if its resampler conditions on the full state the design used.

  2. 2.

    We identify pooling amplification, a failure of pooled scores when many sites share an action sequence. It is driven by errors that the sites share along the action contrast—chiefly model misspecification, but also shared noise that lies along the contrast—grows with the number of sites, and is invisible to the usual validation, which ours missed (§5.3).

  3. 3.

    We show that within the randomization test, tempering is merely a choice of statistic, fixed on training data and incapable of affecting validity, and we propose measuring the design effect along the action contrast; when the contrast is shared across sites this reduces to a weighted Kish factor (Proposition 7).

  4. 4.

    We give design-only bounds on what any statistic can achieve, computable from the command records before any outcome is opened (Proposition 4); they are elementary, but they tell an analyst in advance whether an experiment can yield evidence at all.

  5. 5.

    We report a complete, preregistered validation pipeline for world-model action tests on real experiments, including its failures, with every reported number generated from committed, hashed result files.

Related work.

Randomization tests for experiments in which treatments act over time are established: exact tests of the sharp null of no temporal causal effect, with lag-pp causal estimands, for time-series experiments (Bojinov and Shephard, 2019); conditional randomization tests of partially sharp nulls indexed by a lag in stepped-wedge trials, and by a distance for spillover (Zhang and Zhao, 2025); and tests of the carryover horizon and of non-anticipation in switchback experiments (Liu and Zhong, 2026). The use of machine-learning predictions as randomization-test statistics is also established (Tansey et al., 2022; Ham et al., 2024; Guo et al., 2025); we use both and claim neither. E-values and testing by betting (Shafer, 2021; Vovk and Wang, 2021; Ramdas et al., 2023; Grünwald et al., 2024a) give the aggregation we rely on; model-X conditional-independence tests with e-values (Grünwald et al., 2024b) and sequential Monte Carlo tests (Fischer and Ramdas, 2025) are close relatives. The tempering formulas are standard; §3.4 and §3.5 give their sources, and the contrast factor resembles the score-based rescalings used in composite likelihood. Criticism of permutation-based feature importance for forcing extrapolation (Hooker et al., 2021; Borgonovo et al., 2026) and work on causal confusion, copycat behaviour and policy confounding in imitation and reinforcement learning identify related shortcuts; those works ask whether a policy has learned the wrong cue and repair it with targeted interventions (de Haan et al., 2019), adversarial removal of the nuisance information (Wen et al., 2020), or a broader distribution of trajectories (Suau et al., 2024), whereas we ask whether a world model’s action channel reflects an effect and use only the known design, with finite-sample error control. Design-respecting world models (Yu and Liu, 2026) and advantage-style action channels that contrast a world model’s predictions across actions (Li et al., 2026) are conceptually adjacent. In biology, randomized optogenetic stimulation has been used for causal inference (Loewinger et al., 2026); we analyze two published optogenetics datasets (Nałęcz-Jawecki et al., 2023; Lugagne et al., 2024), released as Nałęcz-Jawecki et al. (2022) and Lugagne et al. (2023).

Organization.

Section 2 sets up units, sites, designs and nulls; §3 gives the test and the tempered statistics; §4 states the theory. Sections 5–7 report synthetic validation, pooling amplification and its repair, and the stand-in trap; §8 reports the real-data evidence; §9 discusses limitations. The appendices give proofs, design laws, all tables and disclosures, and the registrations and hashes.

2 Problem setup

2.1 Units, sites and actions

We observe assignment units i=1,…,Ni=1,\dots,N at discrete times tt. At each time unit ii receives an action Ai,t∈𝒜A_{i,t}\in\mathcal{A}, and outcomes Yi,c,tY_{i,c,t} are recorded at each of its measurement sites c∈𝒞ic\in\mathcal{C}_{i}. All sites of a unit share the unit’s action sequence: actions are assigned to units, not to sites. This distinction matters throughout the paper. In the CcaS/CcaR optogenetic experiment a unit is one cell lineage with a single site; in the ERK experiment a unit is a microscope field, and its sites are the hundreds of cells that receive the same light program; in a pixel world model a unit is an episode and its sites are pixels.

Write a=(aj,s)a=(a_{j,s}) for a complete assignment of actions to all units and times, and Yi,c,s​(a)Y_{i,c,s}(a) for the corresponding potential outcome. We assume no anticipation: Yi,c,s​(a)Y_{i,c,s}(a) depends on aa only through (aj,r)r≤s(a_{j,r})_{r\leq s}. Observed outcomes are Yi,c,s=Yi,c,s​(A)Y_{i,c,s}=Y_{i,c,s}(A). For an origin tt and a horizon h≥1h\geq 1, the future block of unit ii is Ai,tF=(Ai,t+1,…,Ai,t+h)A^{F}_{i,t}=(A_{i,t+1},\dots,A_{i,t+h}) and the targets are Yi,c,t+hY_{i,c,t+h}. Let ℱt\mathcal{F}_{t} denote the observed joint history up to tt: all units’ outcomes and actions up to tt, the clock, and any further covariates that are functions of the past.

2.2 Randomized open-loop design

Assumption 1 (Design).

For every origin tt, conditionally on ℱt\mathcal{F}_{t} and on all potential outcomes,

A⋅,tF∼∏iQi,t,A^{F}_{\cdot,t}\;\sim\;\textstyle\prod_{i}Q_{i,t},

where Qi,tQ_{i,t} is a known law over future blocks that depends only on unit ii’s own past actions Ai,≤tA_{i,\leq t} and on a design stratum fixed in advance.

Assumption 1 states that actions were generated by an open-loop randomized program that did not look at outcomes. We call Qi,tQ_{i,t} the design law. In the experiments we analyze it is reconstructed from the published protocol and acquisition code (Appendix C); every validity statement is conditional on that reconstruction, which we call a working law, and approximate laws are treated in §4. Two features of the design law matter below. First, Qi,tQ_{i,t} may depend on the unit’s entire action history, typically far more of it than a predictive model conditions on. Second, a unit whose design is deterministic at tt (a zero-entropy law) carries no randomization information, and contributes an e-value of exactly one.

2.3 Partial sharp nulls

Definition 1 (Global sharp-in-future null).

H0G​(h)H_{0}^{G}(h): for every unit ii, site cc and origin tt, Yi,c,t+h​(a)=Yi,c,t+h​(a′)Y_{i,c,t+h}(a)=Y_{i,c,t+h}(a^{\prime}) whenever aa and a′a^{\prime} differ only in the future blocks a⋅,tFa^{F}_{\cdot,t} of any units.

Definition 2 (Own-channel null).

Given a spillover graph 𝒩\mathcal{N} on units, H0own​(h,𝒩)H_{0}^{\mathrm{own}}(h;\mathcal{N}): for every unit ii, site cc and origin tt, Yi,c,t+h​(a)Y_{i,c,t+h}(a) is unchanged when ai,tFa^{F}_{i,t} alone is changed. Future actions of 𝒩\mathcal{N}-neighbours may affect Yi,c,t+hY_{i,c,t+h}; units that are not neighbours have no effect.

Both nulls are sharp: they constrain every unit’s potential outcomes, not an average effect. A rejection therefore means that some site responds to some future action, not that the response is large or typical. Both are partial: they concern only the effect of the next hh actions on the outcome at t+ht+h. Actions before the window may have arbitrary effects—this is the dependence that makes action-conditioned prediction possible. At the same target times, the null for horizon hh therefore implies the null for every shorter horizon, but not for a longer one, whose window includes earlier actions. Shared noise of any form, across sites or across units, is allowed. Rejecting H0GH_{0}^{G} means only that global future-action invariance fails; attributing an effect to a unit’s own actions requires H0ownH_{0}^{\mathrm{own}} and its layout assumptions. Conditional randomization tests of partially sharp nulls are not new: Zhang and Zhao (2025) test nulls indexed by a time lag for lagged treatment effects in stepped-wedge trials, assuming no interference and no anticipation, and nulls indexed by a distance threshold for the range of spillover effects; our contribution is not the null, but the analysis of what goes wrong when it is tested with learned models (§2.4 and §3.3).

Admissible statistics.

A statistic for unit ii at origin tt may use any ℱt\mathcal{F}_{t}-measurable covariate, unit ii’s own targets Yi,c,t+hY_{i,c,t+h}, and unit ii’s candidate future block, and nothing else. In particular, no statistic may use other units’ future actions, and under H0ownH_{0}^{\mathrm{own}} none may use other units’ targets, which can respond to unit ii’s future actions through spillover. This is a requirement to be verified for each dataset, not an assumption: in the CcaS release, for example, the neighbour-exposure covariate is aligned one step ahead of the neighbours’ commands and must be replaced by its lag (Appendix C). Which sites contribute at an origin is determined by an observation mask (finite own history and target). That this mask does not respond to future actions under the null is a stated assumption about the measurement process; formally, the measurement process, including any randomness in it, is part of the potential outcomes on which Assumption 1 conditions.

2.4 Stand-in effects

An action-conditioned world model predicts Yi,c,t+hY_{i,c,t+h} from a finite window of the past together with the future block. Under an autocorrelated design the future block is correlated with actions that precede the window, and those earlier actions may affect the target through the system’s memory. The future block then carries information about the target that the window lacks, even when H0GH_{0}^{G} holds: future actions act as a stand-in for omitted history. A model trained to predict will use this information, and its predictions will change when the future block is changed.

Common action diagnostics read this change as an action effect. They compare predictions under the observed block with predictions under inputs that break the stand-in dependence—an all-zero block, a block taken from another unit or another time, or a model retrained without actions—and report an effect when the prediction loss rises. We call all of them replacement diagnostics (the pixel protocol of §7 and Appendix G calls them common diagnostics). Nothing in these comparisons controls how often they do so when no effect exists, and a model that predicts better learns the stand-in better. Proposition 6 gives a construction in which the zero-block, other-unit and retraining diagnostics report an “effect” with probability tending to one under H0GH_{0}^{G}; blocks taken from another time of the same unit are not covered by it.

The design law removes the problem. Blocks drawn from Qi,t(⋅∣Ai,≤t)Q_{i,t}(\cdot\mid A_{i,\leq t}) are correlated with the unit’s earlier actions exactly as the observed block is, so they carry the same stand-in information. Under H0GH_{0}^{G} and Assumption 1, the observed block is exchangeable with such draws given ℱt\mathcal{F}_{t} and the targets, and no statistic can separate them except by chance. The conditioning is essential: resampling from a law that ignores part of the state the design used—for example, the marginal frequency of each action—breaks the stand-in dependence again and reproduces the false effect (§7).

3 Method

A predictor ff is trained and frozen, on units whose data do not depend on the test units’ tested actions, before any test outcome is used, and it enters the test only through a statistic. The design law, not the model, controls the error rate; the model determines power.

3.1 Scores and per-origin e-values

For unit ii and origin tt, let 𝒞i,t⊆𝒞i\mathcal{C}_{i,t}\subseteq\mathcal{C}_{i} be the sites whose own history and target are observed, and let ni,t=|𝒞i,t|n_{i,t}=|\mathcal{C}_{i,t}|. For a candidate block aa, define the site log score and the pooled unit score

ℓi,c,t​(a)=log⁡max⁡{ε,pf​(Yi,c,t+h∣Hi,c,t,a)},Si,t​(a)=∑c∈𝒞i,tℓi,c,t​(a),\ell_{i,c,t}(a)=\log\max\bigl\{\varepsilon,\;p_{f}\bigl(Y_{i,c,t+h}\mid H_{i,c,t},\,a\bigr)\bigr\},\qquad S_{i,t}(a)=\sum_{c\in\mathcal{C}_{i,t}}\ell_{i,c,t}(a), (1)

where Hi,c,tH_{i,c,t} is the site’s admissible history and pfp_{f} is the model’s predictive density. All our reference models use a Gaussian density whose variance, like the floor ε\varepsilon, is fixed on training data; the floor is applied per site before summing. The pooled score is the independence log-likelihood of the unit’s sites (Chandler and Bate, 2007). It treats sites as independent, but validity does not rest on that.

For any admissible statistic Ti,t​(a)T_{i,t}(a)—the pooled score, or the tempered scores of §3.4—the exact and Monte Carlo (MC) e-values at (i,t)(i,t) are

ei,tex\displaystyle e^{\mathrm{ex}}_{i,t} =exp⁡Ti,t​(Ai,tF)∑aQi,t​(a)​exp⁡Ti,t​(a),\displaystyle=\frac{\exp T_{i,t}(A^{F}_{i,t})}{\sum_{a}Q_{i,t}(a)\,\exp T_{i,t}(a)}, (2)
ei,tmc\displaystyle e^{\mathrm{mc}}_{i,t} =(B+1)​exp⁡Ti,t​(Ai,tF)exp⁡Ti,t​(Ai,tF)+∑b=1Bexp⁡Ti,t​(Ai,t(b)),Ai,t(1),…,Ai,t(B)​∼iid​Qi,t.\displaystyle=\frac{(B+1)\,\exp T_{i,t}(A^{F}_{i,t})}{\exp T_{i,t}(A^{F}_{i,t})+\sum_{b=1}^{B}\exp T_{i,t}(A^{(b)}_{i,t})},\qquad A^{(1)}_{i,t},\dots,A^{(B)}_{i,t}\overset{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim}Q_{i,t}. (3)

The numerator scores the observed future actions; the denominator averages the score over the design. This is the conditional randomization test (Candès et al., 2018), with the design law in the role of the known conditional law, written as an e-value. Under H0GH_{0}^{G} and Assumption 1, the observed block is distributed as Qi,tQ_{i,t} given ℱt\mathcal{F}_{t} and the targets (under H0ownH_{0}^{\mathrm{own}}: given ℱt\mathcal{F}_{t}, the future blocks of units outside the independent set, and the targets of the units in it), and the statistic is a fixed function of the candidate block given these. Both e-values therefore have conditional mean one (Proposition 1). The MC form is valid because it includes the observed score in its denominator, which also caps it at B+1B+1. Identical candidate blocks may be merged with their multiplicities, and a zero-entropy design gives e≡1e\equiv 1, as does an origin at which no site is eligible, since the pooled and tempered scores are then identically zero (the tempered score is read as zero there even where its factor would be undefined); statements about the field mean and the site average concern nonempty site sets. We use the exact form when the block space can be enumerated and the MC form otherwise.

3.2 Aggregation

Origins are grouped into residue classes r∈{0,…,h−1}r\in\{0,\dots,h-1\} by t≡r(modh)t\equiv r\pmod{h}. Within a class, consecutive origins are hh apart, so their future blocks do not overlap and each factor is determined by the history at the next origin of the class and the Monte Carlo draws used at its own origin; the factors therefore multiply into an e-value along the class (Proposition 1). Under H0GH_{0}^{G} the joint design also allows multiplication across units:

Er=∏i∏k:tk≡r⁡(mod​h)ei,tk,E=1h∑r=0h−1Er.E_{r}=\prod_{i}\;\prod_{k:\,t_{k}\equiv r\ (\mathrm{mod}\ h)}e_{i,t_{k}},\qquad E=\frac{1}{h}\sum_{r=0}^{h-1}E_{r}. (4)

Averages of e-values are e-values without any independence assumption (Vovk and Wang, 2021). For H0ownH_{0}^{\mathrm{own}} the product over units is taken within each independent set of the spillover graph, and the set products are averaged; without a known graph, singletons are used.

With KK reference models we aggregate each model completely and then average the models’ e-values, E=K−1​∑kE(k)E=K^{-1}\sum_{k}E^{(k)}. Because E≥maxk⁡E(k)/KE\geq\max_{k}E^{(k)}/K, the average loses at most log⁡K\log K in log⁡E\log E relative to the best model chosen in hindsight, so no model selection is needed. We reject at level α\alpha iff E≥1/αE\geq 1/\alpha and report p=min⁡(1,1/E)p=\min(1,1/E); for mm prespecified hypotheses we use the e-Bonferroni rule E≥m/αE\geq m/\alpha (Markov’s inequality and a union bound). Where the registration specifies it, we also report a secondary batch randomization p-value at one prespecified common origin, resampling all units jointly under H0GH_{0}^{G}, or the units of one prespecified independent set under H0ownH_{0}^{\mathrm{own}}.

3.3 The statistic is a free choice

The validity argument uses only two facts: the observed block is distributed as Qi,tQ_{i,t} given ℱt\mathcal{F}_{t} and the targets (under H0ownH_{0}^{\mathrm{own}}: given ℱt\mathcal{F}_{t}, the future blocks of units outside the independent set, and the targets of the units in it), and the statistic is fixed once these and the training data are fixed. Every admissible statistic therefore yields a valid test. Choosing the statistic is a question of power alone, and it may be settled by any procedure that uses neither test outcomes nor the test units’ realised future actions—for example, selection on training units or on synthetic data.

Pooling amplification.

The pooled score is the natural choice, and it fails in a characteristic way. Since the denominator of (2) is at least any one of its terms, for every block a′a^{\prime} with Qi,t​(a′)>0Q_{i,t}(a^{\prime})>0,

log⁡ei,tex≤−[Ti,t​(a′)−Ti,t​(Ai,tF)]−log⁡Qi,t​(a′),\log e^{\mathrm{ex}}_{i,t}\;\leq\;-\bigl[T_{i,t}(a^{\prime})-T_{i,t}(A^{F}_{i,t})\bigr]-\log Q_{i,t}(a^{\prime}), (5)

and the MC form obeys log⁡ei,tmc≤log⁡(B+1)−log⁡K⁡(a′)−[Ti,t​(a′)−Ti,t​(Ai,tF)]\log e^{\mathrm{mc}}_{i,t}\leq\log(B+1)-\log K(a^{\prime})-[T_{i,t}(a^{\prime})-T_{i,t}(A^{F}_{i,t})] for every drawn block a′a^{\prime}, where K⁡(a′)≥1K(a^{\prime})\geq 1 is the number of times a′a^{\prime} occurs among the B+1B+1 blocks. For the pooled score the bracket is a sum over the ni,tn_{i,t} sites. If the per-site score differences ℓi,c,t​(a′)−ℓi,c,t​(Ai,tF)\ell_{i,c,t}(a^{\prime})-\ell_{i,c,t}(A^{F}_{i,t}) have an average over sites bounded away from zero for some block a′a^{\prime} whose design probability does not shrink as sites are added—because the model errs along the action contrast in a direction the sites share—the bound decreases at least linearly in ni,tn_{i,t}, whatever the strength of the true effect. Independent site errors partly cancel in the sum; common errors do not. The pooled e-value thus behaves like an all-in bet on the model’s top-ranked block: valid, but with log⁡E\log E driven far below zero as sites are added. We call this failure pooling amplification.

Errors common to the sites along the contrast arise in two ways. A misspecified model can err in its predicted response to the action, which all sites of a unit share; and noise shared by the sites can lie along the contrast, as when field-wide fluctuations move all cells in the direction an action would. Shared noise orthogonal to the contrast does not amplify. In the pixel world of §6, a correctly specified model is unaffected by both forms of shared noise we simulate, while the fitted models collapse under every noise condition; the cause there is misspecification.

3.4 Tempered scores

We temper the pooled score,

Ti,t​(a)=λi,t​Si,t​(a),0<λi,t≤1,T_{i,t}(a)=\lambda_{i,t}\,S_{i,t}(a),\qquad 0<\lambda_{i,t}\leq 1, (6)

with λi,t\lambda_{i,t} a function of training data and of the site count ni,tn_{i,t} only. The count is determined by the observation mask. Under the stated assumption that the mask does not respond to the tested blocks under the null (§2.3), λi,t\lambda_{i,t} is fixed given the conditioning field of Proposition 1, so (6) is admissible and Proposition 1 applies unchanged. (The same assumption is already needed for the pooled score, whose site set is the mask; if the mask responded to the tested blocks, neither score would be covered. The restriction λ≤1\lambda\leq 1 is not needed for validity.) Setting λ=1\lambda=1 recovers the pooled score, and λ→0\lambda\to 0 gives e→1e\to 1; 1/λi,t1/\lambda_{i,t} can be read as the number of sites that together carry one site’s worth of independent evidence about the action.

Tempering a log-likelihood in this way has a long history: Kish’s design effect for clustered samples (Kish, 1965), adjustments that rescale independence and composite log-likelihoods so that likelihood-ratio statistics recover their usual reference distribution (Chandler and Bate, 2007; Varin et al., 2011; Pace et al., 2011), and learning rates or power likelihoods for misspecified Bayesian models (Grünwald and van Ommen, 2017; Holmes and Walker, 2017). We claim no novelty for the formulas below.

Kish tempering (registered).

With ρ^\hat{\rho} an estimate of the correlation between sites’ residuals,

λi,tK=11+(ni,t−1)​ρ^,\lambda^{\mathrm{K}}_{i,t}=\frac{1}{1+(n_{i,t}-1)\,\hat{\rho}}, (7)

the inverse design effect of a cluster of ni,tn_{i,t} sites with intraclass correlation ρ^\hat{\rho}. In the ERK analyses ρ^\hat{\rho} is computed separately for each reference model and horizon from training-field validation residuals only: Pearson correlations between the residual series of each pair of sites over their common eligible origins (pairs with fewer than three finite, non-constant matched values are omitted), then the median over pairs within each training field, the median over training fields, and clipping to [0,1][0,1]. The pixel simulation uses the same estimator on standardized validation residuals, with episodes in place of fields. This statistic was selected on synthetic data from three candidates under a rule committed before the evaluation; all three reached full power, the deciding comparison was narrow, and one tie-resolution detail of the rule was fixed only in code committed after the evaluation (§6). It is the statistic registered for the confirmatory test M5 (§8).

Contrast tempering (exploratory).

Kish tempering measures how strongly residuals are correlated across sites. Amplification, however, depends on how strongly the sites’ contributions to the score difference between candidate blocks are correlated. For a Gaussian score with predicted mean μc,t​(a)\mu_{c,t}(a) and site variance vcv_{c}, replacing the observed block by a design draw aba^{b} lowers the site log score, to first order in the mean and when the per-site floor is inactive, by

zc,tb=rc,t​Dc,tbvc,rc,t=Yc,t+h−μc,t​(AtF),Dc,tb=μc,t​(AtF)−μc,t​(ab),z^{b}_{c,t}=\frac{r_{c,t}\,D^{b}_{c,t}}{v_{c}},\qquad r_{c,t}=Y_{c,t+h}-\mu_{c,t}(A^{F}_{t}),\qquad D^{b}_{c,t}=\mu_{c,t}(A^{F}_{t})-\mu_{c,t}(a^{b}),

where Dc,tbD^{b}_{c,t} is the action contrast. The contrast-tempering factor is the ratio of the mean square that the pooled score implicitly assumes for the sum of these contributions (independent sites) to their actual mean square, estimated on validation data with BcB_{c} design draws ab∼Qta^{b}\sim Q_{t} per origin:

λc=∑t,b∑c(zc,tb)2∑t,b(∑czc,tb)2,clipped to ​[1/n, 1].\lambda^{\mathrm{c}}=\frac{\sum_{t,b}\sum_{c}\bigl(z^{b}_{c,t}\bigr)^{2}}{\sum_{t,b}\bigl(\sum_{c}z^{b}_{c,t}\bigr)^{2}},\qquad\text{clipped to }[1/n,\,1]. (8)

It is computed once per model and setting from validation episodes only, and is written and hashed before any test e-value is computed. The ratio is defined when its denominator is positive. If the contributions have zero cross moments across sites, its expected numerator and denominator agree; the ratio itself need not have expectation one, but it tends to one when the two sums, suitably normalized, satisfy a law of large numbers with a common positive limit. If the contributions are identical across a common number nn of sites, it equals 1/n1/n. The two factors can disagree in either direction. When a model misplaces a moving object, its residuals take both signs across pixels and their pairwise correlation averages to nearly zero, so λK≈1\lambda^{\mathrm{K}}\approx 1; weighted by the contrast, which has the same spatial pattern as the error, the same residuals add coherently, and λc≪1\lambda^{\mathrm{c}}\ll 1. Conversely, a frame-wide offset makes residuals strongly correlated, so λK\lambda^{\mathrm{K}} is small, but the offset is orthogonal to a contrast that moves intensity without changing its total, so λc≈1\lambda^{\mathrm{c}}\approx 1. Contrast tempering was declared in the simulation protocol, before the pixel experiment was run, as an exploratory generalization; it has had no confirmatory test.

When Kish tempering suffices.

If the action contrast is the same at every site and the site variances are equal—as for an additive model whose action branch sees only the unit’s shared actions, the form of the ERK reference models—the contrast factor (8), where defined, satisfies the weighted cross-product identity of Proposition 7; for a common site count it has the form of a Kish factor whose correlation is a contrast-weighted ratio of uncentred residual cross-products, which is not in general the median-of-Pearson estimate in (7).

3.5 A betting reading

In the exact form, ei,t=Qi,tT​(Ai,tF)/Qi,t​(Ai,tF)e_{i,t}=Q^{T}_{i,t}(A^{F}_{i,t})/Q_{i,t}(A^{F}_{i,t}) with Qi,tT​(a)∝Qi,t​(a)​eTi,t​(a)Q^{T}_{i,t}(a)\propto Q_{i,t}(a)\,e^{T_{i,t}(a)}. The e-value is the likelihood ratio of an alternative design law that up-weights blocks the model scores highly—equivalently, the wealth multiplier of a bet against the null placed according to the model (Shafer, 2021; Ramdas et al., 2023; Grünwald et al., 2024a). Tempering replaces this alternative by

Qi,tλ​S∝Qi,t 1−λ​(Qi,tS)λ,Q^{\lambda S}_{i,t}\;\propto\;Q_{i,t}^{\,1-\lambda}\,\bigl(Q^{S}_{i,t}\bigr)^{\lambda},

a geometric interpolation between the null law and the pooled bet. Fractional Kelly betting (MacLean et al., 1992; MacLean et al., 2010), advocated when one is not confident about the alternative (Ramdas et al., 2023), instead mixes arithmetically, Qκ=(1−κ)​Q+κ​QSQ_{\kappa}=(1-\kappa)\,Q+\kappa\,Q^{S}, which gives e=1−κ+κ​eSe=1-\kappa+\kappa\,e^{S}; we include it, with κ=1/2\kappa=1/2 applied per origin, as a reference arm in §6. Both shrink the alternative toward the null as a guard against misspecification, and both keep the pooled bet’s ranking of blocks. They interpolate along different paths: tempering along the exponential family Qλ​SQ^{\lambda S}, fractional Kelly along the mixture family QκQ_{\kappa}. Geometric shrinkage rescales the score: when per-site score differences are bounded, a factor λ\lambda of order 1/n1/n removes the linear growth of |log⁡e||\log e| in the number of sites; arithmetic mixing bounds each factor below by 1−κ1-\kappa. When the score takes only two values on the support of QQ (for example, a single binary action) the two families coincide, each λ\lambda matching an origin-specific κ\kappa. With three or more distinct score values they differ at every interior parameter, 0<λ<10<\lambda<1, although they share their endpoints; the two are different members of one family of defences.

3.6 Statistics used in this paper

Table 1 lists every statistic that appears in the paper, with its label in the registered and protocol documents and its evidential status. Under the conditions of Proposition 1 they give valid tests and differ only in power. The pooled and tempered scores are admissible statistics in (2)–(3); the field-mean and oracle variants of §6 are too, on their defined domains, when their candidate scores use only the unit’s own history, targets and candidate block; the site average averages, over a nonempty site set fixed in the null conditioning, the per-site e-values that these equations give; and fractional Kelly averages an e-value with the constant one. Averages of e-values are again e-values. The full definitions of the variants are in the frozen protocols and are not restated here.

Notation in the registered documents.

The registered M4 documents write λ\lambda for the precision 1/(2​σ2)1/(2\sigma^{2}) of the Gaussian score; in this paper λ\lambda denotes only the tempering factor. The labels C1–C5 of the sealed-challenge criteria (§5) are unrelated to the statistic labels in Table 1. The specification writes GtG_{t} for the observed history and 𝒢\mathcal{G} for the spillover graph; we write ℱt\mathcal{F}_{t} and 𝒩\mathcal{N}.

4 Theory

The statements below restate the obligations of the registered specification, whose labels are given in parentheses, with notation adapted and with the hypotheses that the frozen proofs use stated explicitly. The proofs are in Appendix B. They follow the theory documents that were written before the registration and frozen with it (Appendix B lists them with their hashes), and Appendix B marks each place where we have added a hypothesis or tightened an argument; none of these changes affects the registered method. Proposition 7 is new in this paper and was not part of the registration. Every guarantee is conditional on the design law used for resampling being the law that generated the actions; §4.3 treats departures from it.

4.1 Validity

Proposition 1 (Validity; P1(a)–(c)).

Suppose Assumption 1 holds at every origin, and that

  1. (i)

    the units, origins and sites that enter each product are fixed by structural events (layout, design allocation) that do not depend on the tested blocks, by own-path eligibility events treated in Proposition 2(b), or by the observation mask, which under the null in force does not respond to the tested blocks (§2.3);

  2. (ii)

    the predictor and every score parameter (floor, variance, tempering factor) are functions of the observation mask and of training information that is conditionally independent of the joint vector of tested blocks given ℱt\mathcal{F}_{t} and the potential outcomes;

  3. (iii)

    Monte Carlo draws are generated from Qi,tQ_{i,t} at the realised past, with randomness independent of the potential outcomes, of the assignments, and across units and origins.

Then:

  1. (a)

    Under H0G​(h)H_{0}^{G}(h), conditionally on ℱt\mathcal{F}_{t}, the potential outcomes and the targets at t+ht+h of all units, each exact or MC factor has mean one, and so does their product across units. Along each residue grid the running product is a non-negative martingale with initial value one, with respect to the filtration generated by the history at the grid origins, the frozen training and design information, and the Monte Carlo seeds already used.

  2. (b)

    Under H0own​(h,𝒩)H_{0}^{\mathrm{own}}(h;\mathcal{N}), let II be an independent set of 𝒩\mathcal{N} fixed before testing, and let the statistic of each i∈Ii\in I use, besides ℱt\mathcal{F}_{t}-measurable covariates and its own candidate block, only unit ii’s own targets. Then, conditionally on ℱt\mathcal{F}_{t}, the potential outcomes, the future blocks of the units outside II and the targets of the units in II, each exact or MC factor of a unit in II has mean one, and so does their product over II; along each residue grid the running product over II is a martingale as in (a). The conditioning may not include the targets of units outside II: through spillover these can depend on the blocks in II.

  3. (c)

    Prechosen arithmetic averages over residue classes, independent sets and models of the quantities in (a)–(b) are e-values at the fixed analysis time, so Pr⁡(E≥1/α)≤α\Pr(E\geq 1/\alpha)\leq\alpha. A batch randomization p-value computed at one prespecified common origin, with a statistic that is a fixed function of the joint candidate block given the conditioning field of (a) (respectively (b)), resampling all units jointly under H0GH_{0}^{G} or the units of one independent set under H0ownH_{0}^{\mathrm{own}}, and counting ties as exceedances, is super-uniform.

The argument is short. Under H0GH_{0}^{G} and no anticipation, the targets at t+ht+h are functions of the potential-outcome functions and of the actions up to tt, so conditioning on them leaves the design law of the tested blocks unchanged. The denominator of (2) is then the conditional expectation of its numerator; in the MC form, the observed block and its draws are exchangeable and the observed share of the total score has mean 1/(B+1)1/(B+1). Shared outcome noise is part of the potential outcomes and requires no independence. A factor at a grid origin tkt_{k} is determined by the history at tk+1=tk+ht_{k+1}=t_{k}+h and the MC draws used at tkt_{k}, which gives the martingale; averages of e-values are e-values without independence (Vovk and Wang, 2021). Under H0ownH_{0}^{\mathrm{own}} the targets of units in an independent set are invariant to the set’s own blocks but those of neighbours outside it need not be, which is why (b) conditions on, and scores with, only the set’s own targets. Two limits are worth stating. Optional stopping is licensed only along a single residue grid (by Ville’s inequality); the average over classes is a fixed-time e-value, not an e-process on a common clock. And nothing in the argument depends on the predictor’s accuracy, on independence between sites, or on the noise distribution: these affect power only.

Proposition 2 (Eligibility; P1(d), P1(e)).
  1. (a)

    Let the structural eligibility events not depend on the tested blocks, and run the structural and the classifier-based pipelines with the same statistics and the same Monte Carlo draws whenever their eligible sets coincide. If the event that any classifier decision differs from its structural event has probability at most δ\delta under the law that generated the commands, the classifier-based test has size at most min⁡(1,α+δ)\min(1,\alpha+\delta). The bound is unconditional over repetitions of the experiment and classifier; it is not a guarantee conditional on the selected set.

  2. (b)

    Suppose Assumption 1 holds at every origin. Let unit ii be analysed only on an event ℰi\mathcal{E}_{i} that is a fixed function of its own complete action path, chosen before the data and depending on no other unit’s actions and on no outcome (for example, that the path avoids prespecified fixed templates). Suppose that every unit on which ℰi\mathcal{E}_{i} holds follows QiQ_{i} (the template list contains every fixed design), and that Pr⁡(ℰi∣Ai,≤t)>0\Pr(\mathcal{E}_{i}\mid A_{i,\leq t})>0 at every analysed origin. Then replacing Qi,tQ_{i,t} by Qi,t(⋅∣ℰi,Ai,≤t)Q_{i,t}(\cdot\mid\mathcal{E}_{i},A_{i,\leq t}) keeps Proposition 1 exact, conditionally on the eligibility pattern of all units. For a hidden-Markov design this conditional law is computed exactly by a forward–backward recursion on the hidden state augmented with template-match indicators.

Part (b) is used for the CcaS random-walk lineages, whose resampling law is conditioned on not reproducing either duplicated fixed template; lineages that reproduce a template are excluded (Appendix C). Part (a) enters only the secondary own-channel analyses; with no independent record of the physical layout, the only bound we can establish is δ≤1\delta\leq 1, and we display it as vacuous next to every such result.

Proposition 3 (Distributional nulls do not compose; P1b).

Let (A1,k,A2,k,Uk)(A_{1,k},A_{2,k},U_{k}), k=1,2,3k=1,2,3, be independent fair bits, drawn afresh at each of three origins; take horizon h=1h=1 and design law Q=(12,12)Q=(\tfrac{1}{2},\tfrac{1}{2}). Consider the systems (i) Y1,k=UkY_{1,k}=U_{k}, Y2,k=Uk⊕A1,k⊕A2,kY_{2,k}=U_{k}\oplus A_{1,k}\oplus A_{2,k}, and (ii) Yi,k=Ai,k⊕UkY_{i,k}=A_{i,k}\oplus U_{k}, i=1,2i=1,2. In both, for every unit ii and origin kk, Ai,kA_{i,k} is independent of Yi,kY_{i,k} given both units’ earlier actions and outcomes and the other unit’s actions, so each unit-wise conditional-independence null holds and each unit-wise e-process has mean one. Score each unit by the Gaussian density 𝒩⁡(Yi,k,Ai,k,σ2)\mathcal{N}(Y_{i,k};A_{i,k},\sigma^{2}) with σ2=1/(2​log⁡9)\sigma^{2}=1/(2\log 9), so that the matching bit is nine times as likely as the other and each exact factor equals 9/59/5 or 1/51/5. Then the product of the unit-wise e-values across both units and the three origins has mean 1.643≈4.411.64^{3}\approx 4.41 and exact rejection probability 1/81/8 at α=0.05\alpha=0.05.

The value 1/81/8 is the probability that all six factors equal 9/59/5; among density ratios r≥1r\geq 1 it holds exactly when r≥201/6/(2−201/6)≈4.675r\geq 20^{1/6}/(2-20^{1/6})\approx 4.675, and the rejection probability is zero for 1≤r<4.6751\leq r<4.675. Fresh noise is part of the construction: if UU were drawn once and held fixed, earlier outcomes would reveal it, and after the first origin the unit-wise null would fail for unit 2 in system (i) and for both units in system (ii). Both systems violate the sharp nulls, so for our tests they are alternatives. The proposition explains why the product across units in Proposition 1(a) needs a sharp null: unit-wise distributional statements say nothing about how one unit’s action enters another unit’s outcome.

4.2 What the design permits

Proposition 4 (Design limits; P2(a)–(e), regrouped).
  1. (a)

    [P2(a), P2(c)] Pathwise,

    ei,tex≤1Qi,t​(Ai,tF),ei,tmc≤B+11+K,e^{\mathrm{ex}}_{i,t}\leq\frac{1}{Q_{i,t}(A^{F}_{i,t})},\qquad e^{\mathrm{mc}}_{i,t}\leq\frac{B+1}{1+K},

    where KK is the number of draws equal to the observed block. A zero-entropy design gives e≡1e\equiv 1.

  2. (b)

    [P2(b), P2(c)] Under any alternative, the actions still follow the design law, so

    Pr(E≥1/α)≤PrQ(maxcomponents∑factors−logQi,t(Ai,tF)≥log(1/α)),\Pr\bigl(E\geq 1/\alpha\bigr)\;\leq\;\Pr_{Q}\Bigl(\max_{\text{components}}\;\sum_{\text{factors}}-\log Q_{i,t}(A^{F}_{i,t})\;\geq\;\log(1/\alpha)\Bigr),

    the maximum running over residue classes and independent sets, and the probability over coherent full command paths (blocks of different residue classes share actions). The right-hand side is computable from commands alone. With mm prespecified hypotheses the threshold 1/α1/\alpha becomes m/αm/\alpha; under Proposition 2(b), Qi,tQ_{i,t} and PrQ\Pr_{Q} are replaced by their conditioned versions. The MC form has an analogous ceiling, with log⁡(B+1)−log⁡(1+K)\log(B+1)-\log(1+K) in place of −log⁡Q-\log Q and K∼Binomial⁡(B,Qi,t​(Ai,tF))K\sim\mathrm{Binomial}(B,Q_{i,t}(A^{F}_{i,t})); it can exceed the exact-form ceiling.

  3. (c)

    [P2(d)] With 𝒯\mathcal{T} the frozen training information on which the score depends, 𝔼[logei,tex∣ℱt,𝒯]≤I(Y⋅,t+h;Ai,tF∣ℱt,𝒯)≤HQ(Ai,tF∣ℱt)\mathbb{E}\bigl[\log e^{\mathrm{ex}}_{i,t}\mid\mathcal{F}_{t},\mathcal{T}\bigr]\leq I\bigl(Y_{\cdot,t+h};A^{F}_{i,t}\mid\mathcal{F}_{t},\mathcal{T}\bigr)\leq H_{Q}\bigl(A^{F}_{i,t}\mid\mathcal{F}_{t}\bigr).

  4. (d)

    [P2(e)] For the batch test, p≥Qjoint​(AobsF)p\geq Q^{\mathrm{joint}}(A^{F}_{\mathrm{obs}}) in the exact form and p≥(1+K)/(B+1)p\geq(1+K)/(B+1) in the add-one MC form.

Part (a) is one line—the observed term appears in its own denominator—and we do not present it as a deep result. Its value is practical. Parts (a)–(b) tell an analyst, before any outcome is opened, whether any statistic could reach the rejection threshold; a deterministic stimulation protocol yields no evidence whatever the model. Because averaging models adds no design entropy, the same command-only bound applies to the model average. For the ERK analyses (M4, X and M5; Figure 5) we report the exact-form bound log⁡Eupper\log E_{\mathrm{upper}} as a command-only comparator. Those analyses use Monte Carlo e-values, which the exact-form bound does not bound pathwise (part (b)), so the ratio log⁡E/log⁡Eupper\log E/\log E_{\mathrm{upper}} is descriptive: it could in principle exceed one, and it is not a power percentage. Part (c) is a growth statement only.

4.3 Approximate design laws

Proposition 5 (Approximate law; P3).

Suppose the test resamples from a working law Q^\hat{Q} that is fixed independently of the tested blocks, with Q^i,t\hat{Q}_{i,t} depending only on Ai,≤tA_{i,\leq t} and the stratum, while the actions follow QQ (Assumption 1). Let Δ\Delta be the total-variation distance between the laws, under QQ and under Q^\hat{Q}, of the complete command path from the first tested origin on, given the history before it and the frozen training and working-law information; under Assumption 1 these laws do not involve the potential outcomes. Then, under the null,

Pr⁡(E≥1/α)≤α+𝔼⁡[Δ].\Pr(E\geq 1/\alpha)\;\leq\;\alpha+\mathbb{E}[\Delta].

If moreover 0≤E≤M0\leq E\leq M, then 𝔼⁡[E]≤1+M​𝔼​[Δ]\mathbb{E}[E]\leq 1+M\,\mathbb{E}[\Delta].

The event bound needs neither a coupling construction nor a bound on EE. The moment bound, with M=(B+1)mM=(B+1)^{m} for an MC product of mm factors, is weaker whenever rejection is possible (M≥1/αM\geq 1/\alpha). By a telescoping argument over time steps, Δ\Delta is at most the expected sum, along the true command path, of the one-step total-variation distances between the true and working kernels, and for product kernels each one-step distance is at most the sum of the unit distances. It is unknown for the working laws used here, and those laws were not fitted independently of the released commands, so the proposition does not license our real-data tests; we rely instead on calibration with the real command records (§5). The closest published result, Theorem 4 of Berrett et al. (2020), bounds the type I error of the conditional randomization test, conditionally on YY and ZZ, by α\alpha plus the total variation distance between the true and fitted conditional laws of XX given ZZ for the whole sample, for independent and identically distributed data with the statistic and fitted law chosen independently of XX and YY; it covers both the randomization and the permutation forms, and it does not directly cover this longitudinal product. The resampler of §7 that ignores part of the design state is far from the design law in total variation, and nothing in Proposition 5 protects it.

4.4 Why replacement diagnostics fail

Proposition 6 (Failure of replacement diagnostics; P4).

Let the units be independent and identically distributed copies of the following experiment, observed at one fixed clock, with all its parameters fixed as the number of units grows. Each unit has a stratum θi∈{0,1}\theta_{i}\in\{0,1\} known to the design, with Pr⁡(θi=1)∈(0,1)\Pr(\theta_{i}=1)\in(0,1). Let θi\theta_{i} enter only an outcome recorded before the predictor’s window, let the outcomes inside the window be constant, and let the focal outcome be θi\theta_{i} plus independent centred noise of finite variance, for every action assignment, so that H0GH_{0}^{G} holds. Let the actions follow the Markov chain Pr⁡(As=1∣As−1=a)=ρ​a+(1−ρ)​pθi\Pr(A_{s}=1\mid A_{s-1}=a)=\rho a+(1-\rho)p_{\theta_{i}}, started in its stationary law, with 0≤ρ<10\leq\rho<1, p0≠p1p_{0}\neq p_{1} and p0,p1∈(0,1)p_{0},p_{1}\in(0,1). A predictor sees a window WW of finitely many recent commands, the recent outcomes and the clock, together with the future block FF of a fixed length h≥1h\geq 1, but neither θi\theta_{i} nor the earlier outcome; its ideal form is μ=𝔼[Y∣W,F]\mu=\mathbb{E}[Y\mid W,F]. Under squared-error loss, the population risk gaps of (i) retraining without actions (μ0=𝔼⁡[Y∣W]\mu_{0}=\mathbb{E}[Y\mid W], or 𝔼⁡[Y]\mathbb{E}[Y] if the window’s commands are removed as well), (ii) replacing FF by zeros and (iii) replacing FF by the block of an independent unit are strictly positive. For these ideal predictors, as the number of units grows the empirical gaps converge to these constants while unit (for (iii), pair) bootstrap intervals shrink, so each diagnostic reports an effect with probability tending to one. Under the same construction, Proposition 1 bounds by α\alpha the size of the randomization test that resamples from Q(⋅∣Ai,t,θi)Q(\cdot\mid A_{i,t},\theta_{i}).

The window must not reveal the stratum: if the recent outcomes did (for instance, if they equalled θi\theta_{i}), the future block would add nothing and all three gaps would vanish. The proposition concerns ideal predictors, as the frozen proof does; fitted predictors inherit it only under further convergence conditions, which we do not pursue. The construction is the stand-in effect of §2.4 in its simplest form: the future block reveals θi\theta_{i} beyond what the window does, so a good predictor uses it, and a replacement that breaks the dependence costs predictive accuracy without any action effect. Design draws preserve the dependence, which is why the randomization test is unaffected. The proposition covers replacement by another unit’s block, not by a block taken from another time of the same unit. The development simulations confirm the construction numerically (§5).

4.5 Pooling and tempering

Tempering needs no separate validity result: the tempered score (6) is admissible (§3.4), so Proposition 1 applies to it. The bound (5) of §3.3 describes how the pooled score loses power. The remaining question is when the registered Kish factor approximates the contrast factor.

Proposition 7 (Contrast tempering under a shared contrast; new).

If the action contrast is common to the sites, Dc,tb=DtbD^{b}_{c,t}=D^{b}_{t}, the site variances are equal, vc=v>0v_{c}=v>0, the same sites enter every candidate at each origin, and the numerator and denominator of (8) are positive, then the unclipped contrast factor equals 1/(1+X)1/(1+X) with

X=∑twt​∑c≠c′rc,t​rc′,t∑twt​∑crc,t2,wt=∑b(Dtb)2.X=\frac{\sum_{t}w_{t}\sum_{c\neq c^{\prime}}r_{c,t}\,r_{c^{\prime},t}}{\sum_{t}w_{t}\sum_{c}r_{c,t}^{2}},\qquad w_{t}=\sum_{b}\bigl(D^{b}_{t}\bigr)^{2}.

For a common site count n≥2n\geq 2 this is λc=1/[1+(n−1)​ρ¯D]\lambda^{\mathrm{c}}=1/[1+(n-1)\bar{\rho}_{D}] with ρ¯D=X/(n−1)∈(−1/(n−1),1]\bar{\rho}_{D}=X/(n-1)\in(-1/(n-1),1].

Proof.

Under the hypotheses, zc,tb=rc,t​Dtb/vz^{b}_{c,t}=r_{c,t}D^{b}_{t}/v, so ∑c(zc,tb)2=(Dtb/v)2​∑crc,t2\sum_{c}(z^{b}_{c,t})^{2}=(D^{b}_{t}/v)^{2}\sum_{c}r_{c,t}^{2} and (∑czc,tb)2=(Dtb/v)2​[∑crc,t2+∑c≠c′rc,t​rc′,t](\sum_{c}z^{b}_{c,t})^{2}=(D^{b}_{t}/v)^{2}\bigl[\sum_{c}r_{c,t}^{2}+\sum_{c\neq c^{\prime}}r_{c,t}r_{c^{\prime},t}\bigr]. Summing over bb gives the weight wt/v2w_{t}/v^{2} for each origin; dividing the two sums over tt gives the result. ∎

Remark 1.

The identity λc=1/(1+X)\lambda^{\mathrm{c}}=1/(1+X) holds for any site counts. Its reading as a Kish factor with intraclass correlation ρ¯D\bar{\rho}_{D} requires a common site count. When the count ntn_{t} varies across origins, XX is a weighted mean of (nt−1)​ρt(n_{t}-1)\rho_{t}, so the single constant λc\lambda^{\mathrm{c}} corresponds to a Kish factor at an effective site count and need not equal 1/[1+(nt−1)​ρ^]1/[1+(n_{t}-1)\hat{\rho}] at every origin; with at least two distinct counts, equality at every origin requires ρ^=0\hat{\rho}=0 and λc=1\lambda^{\mathrm{c}}=1. For a common nn, clipping λc\lambda^{\mathrm{c}} to [1/n,1][1/n,1] is the same as clipping ρ¯D\bar{\rho}_{D} to [0,1][0,1].

When the contrast is shared, contrast tempering is therefore Kish tempering with a particular estimate of the intraclass correlation: a pooled, contrast-weighted mean of uncentred within-origin residual cross-products, instead of the median of pairwise Pearson correlations used in (7). The two estimate the same correlation only under conditions on the contrast weights as well as on the residuals: for instance, centred, equally variable residuals with an exchangeable and stable correlation, and contrast weights independent of the residuals. Without the condition on the weights, the contrast-weighted correlation can differ from the ordinary one even when the residuals are uncorrelated. The contrast hypothesis holds for additive models whose action branch sees only the unit’s shared inputs; the ERK reference models have this form, so agreement between the two factors on ERK is partly structural. Because ERK site counts vary across fields and origins, the meaningful comparison there is between ρ^\hat{\rho} and the pooled correlation implied by λc\lambda^{\mathrm{c}}, not between λi,tK\lambda^{\mathrm{K}}_{i,t} and a single constant. The ERK training diagnostic (§8.5) finds the implied correlation lower than both the median and the mean of the pairwise correlations, so Kish tempering is somewhat conservative there; it is a description of how these correlation summaries differ, not an independent test of the Kish rule. When the contrast varies across sites, as when an action moves an object across pixels, the hypothesis fails and the two factors can differ in either direction (§3.4, §6).

5 Synthetic validation

Before any real outcome was reopened, the registered pooled statistic passed through four layers of synthetic checks, each fixed before it was run: development simulations with known truth (M2a), calibration on the real command records with synthetic outcomes (M2b), a power pilot and an end-to-end rehearsal (M2c, M2e), and a sealed challenge built in a separate session after the method was frozen (M3). We report what each layer tested and, equally, what it could not have detected. A fifth check, a single-field rehearsal for M5, is described at the end. Full tables are in Appendix D.

5.1 Development simulations

The development grid crossed five design laws (renewal, bounded walk, Markov, clock-locked and shuffle) with linear, saturating and delayed outcome dynamics, for each of the four reference models, with 256 replicates per cell. It contained four null families—the stand-in construction of Proposition 6, sharp-null mutual spillover (an own-channel null), shared noise under the global null, and zero-entropy designs—and two alternatives built from the masked effects of Proposition 3.

Validity.

Across all designs, dynamics and models, the exact and MC e-value tests never rejected in the stand-in family (0/256 for the exact form and 0/256 for the MC form, in every cell), and rejected at most 5/256 under shared noise and 3/256 under sharp-null spillover. The batch randomization p-value at a single origin is a p-value test at level 0.050.05 with B=127B=127, so its attainable nominal rate is 6/1286/128, or 1212 of 256256 replicates. Across the 240 null cells of the grid (60 in each null family) it rejected in at most 20 of 256256 replicates, a count reached in 1 cell, under shared noise; 26 cells exceeded 1212. With this many cells, some counts above 1212 are expected from binomial variation alone. In the largest stand-in setting, with 512512 units, the four models rejected at rates from 4.3% to 6.6%, none significantly above the nominal rate (smallest one-sided binomial tail probability 0.096). Validity means a rejection rate at most α\alpha, not zero rejections; the e-value tests reject far less often than α\alpha because Markov’s inequality is conservative.

The stand-in construction.

In the stand-in family the replacement diagnostics reported an action effect in up to 246/256 (zero block), 249/256 (another unit’s block) and 236/256 (retraining without actions) replicates, although no action had any effect. In the largest setting of the construction every model’s zero-block and swap diagnostics reported an effect in every replicate (minima across models 256/256 for the zero block and 256/256 for the swap), while the e-value tests never rejected (0/256; Figure 4B). The diagnostics fail just as badly in zero-entropy designs, where the actions follow a deterministic schedule and the randomization test returns e≡1e\equiv 1 by construction: there they reported effects in up to 254/256 replicates. A randomization test that resamples from the marginal frequency of each action instead of the design law (B-marg) reported effects in up to 256/256 stand-in replicates, the same failure that §7 reproduces in the pixel world.

Power where the design allows little.

The masked alternatives were built to be hard: their effects are invisible to unit-wise marginal comparisons. The e-value tests rejected in at most 9/256 replicates for masked XOR effects and 97/256 for masked shared effects. We report this as a limitation, not a failure of validity; the sealed challenge reproduces it (§5.4).

5.2 Calibration with the real command records

Proposition 5 does not license tests under working laws whose distance from the true law is unknown, so the working laws were calibrated on the released command records themselves. Each replicate drew a fresh random subset of real command paths and fresh synthetic outcomes from a model satisfying the sharp null, so that the estimated size averages over whatever law generated the released commands while the test resamples from the working law. The pre-committed criterion required the one-sided 95% Clopper–Pearson upper bound on size to be at most 0.060.06 in every primary cell. All 64 of 64 primary cells passed; the largest point false-positive rate was 0.40% and the largest upper bound 1.3%. One generator placed the stand-in construction on the real command records, with a slowly decaying response to past commands and strongly autocorrelated noise; there the test rejected in at most 0.40% of replicates, whereas retraining without actions and zero-block replacement reported effects in up to 92.8% and 91% of them.

5.3 Power pilot and end-to-end rehearsal

On the full M4 grid of origins, all 16 of 16 null cells passed the registered validity gate (largest upper bound 3.1%), and the four-model average had minimum power across cells of 100% at 10%10\% signal and 100% at 30%30\%. At 2%2\% signal, power for ERK at thirty minutes ranged from 4.5% to 71%, which the specification recorded as a limitation. An end-to-end rehearsal of the frozen pipeline on a simple synthetic generator rejected strongly (log⁡E=136\log E=136 at ten minutes).

Neither check could have revealed pooling amplification. The pilot gave each synthetic ERK field a single outcome trajectory, not hundreds of cells sharing one light program, and the rehearsal’s generator was simple enough for the fitted models to be nearly correctly specified. The pooled statistic therefore entered M4 without ever having been scored on many sites that share an action sequence under a misspecified model—precisely the setting in which it fails (§6). We regard this as the main gap in our pre-registration validation.

5.4 Sealed challenge

The sealed challenge was generated in a separate session after the method was frozen and registered, from generators the method author never saw, and scored with the frozen implementation; the analysis functions used were verified identical to those of M4. It comprised 11 families: new designs and dynamics, an omitted-history stand-in construction, spillover on a given graph, shared autoregressive outcome noise, masked XOR effects, a known approximate-law error and zero-entropy designs. Its frozen criteria were a size bound, power where the design permits it, and exact neutrality under zero entropy.

The pooled statistic registered for M4 rejected in 0/3400 null replicates (pooled upper bound 0.088%; largest per-family upper bound 1.5%). Zero-entropy cells returned ee and EE equal to one exactly. Of the 16 alternative cells whose exact design ceiling was at least 0.950.95, 15 reached the required power of 0.800.80. The exception was the masked XOR family, with 24/200 rejections (12%) against a ceiling of 100%. Its effects are sharp but masked marginally, as in the masked alternatives of the development grid (§5.1), which were also the hard case there. As in M2, the replacement diagnostics reported effects at high rates in null families (Figure 6). Two disclosures apply. The challenge’s designer had seen the source of the reference models and one correction to the challenge design. And none of its families was built around units with many sites sharing an action sequence (Appendix D lists them), so, like the pilot, it was not designed to reveal pooling amplification.

5.5 A single-field rehearsal for M5

Before the M5 plan was finalized, the Kish-tempered statistic was rehearsed on synthetic outcomes attached to one real training field’s command path, with the linear-Gaussian model only and the rejection threshold E≥40E\geq 40 of the draft plan, which then had two primary horizons. With the simple synthetic response the statistic rejected in every replicate at both horizons (for example 32/32 at ten minutes with field-wide shared noise). With the harder generator and field-wide shared noise it rejected in 27/32 replicates at ten minutes but only 2/32 at thirty minutes. The registered plan therefore made ten minutes the only primary horizon, with threshold E≥20E\geq 20; because E≥40E\geq 40 implies E≥20E\geq 20, these counts are lower bounds on the rehearsal’s rejections at the registered threshold.

6 Pooling amplification and its repair

The registered M4 analysis failed on its own positive controls (§8.2). This section reports how we diagnosed the failure and selected a repair, on synthetic outcomes attached to the ERK command records, and a pre-declared demonstration of the same failure in a pixel world model. Everything here is exploratory. The diagnosis and the selection used no test outcome, and the repaired statistic was then confirmed on a field that no one had opened (§8.4).

6.1 Diagnosis on ERK-like synthetic data

We attached synthetic outcomes to the command records of the M4 test fields, with five hundred cells per field, and fitted the linear-Gaussian reference model exactly as in M4. Three findings located the failure.

First, the pooled score collapsed without any shared noise. With independent cell noise, its median log⁡E\log E at ten minutes was −-317 at 10%10\% signal and −-1680 at 30%30\%: a stronger effect made the evidence more negative, as (5) predicts when a misspecified model’s error along the contrast grows with the effect it misrepresents. These medians come from the diagnostic runs, with thirty-two replicates per cell; the selection grid of §6.2, with sixteen replicates per cell, gives similar values (Table 6).

Second, the oracle predictor rejected in every replicate (16/16 at ten minutes and 16/16 at thirty), and the pipeline remained valid under the null (0/64 rejections with mean ee 1.00027 on ERK commands, 0/64 with mean ee 0.99998 on CcaS commands). The oracle’s log⁡E\log E of 135 at ten minutes is a ceiling set by ties among resampled blocks—the generator responds only to the last action of the block—and not the design bound of Proposition 4.

Third, changing the pipeline one component at a time showed that a single step caused the collapse: summing the cells’ log scores and then normalizing once over the field’s design (rejections 8/8 before that step, 0/8 after it; Figure 2B). Adding field-wide shared noise to the simple rehearsal generator of §5.3 also collapsed the pooled score (median log⁡E\log E −-10,494 at ten minutes in the selection grid of §6.2): noise shared by all cells moves them in the direction of the contrast, so it amplifies in the same way as model error.

6.2 Selecting a repair

Before evaluating any candidate, we committed a protocol listing three repairs and a selection rule. The candidates were the Kish-tempered score (§3.4), a field-mean score that scores the field-average outcome under a Gaussian whose variance accounts for the within-field correlation, and a site-average that averages per-cell e-values; each kept the design law, the Monte Carlo bags and the aggregation of M4. The grid crossed two generators (the first at two signal levels), two levels of shared noise and both horizons, giving twelve alternative cells with sixteen replicates each, and two null cells with thirty-two replicates each. The rule was: (1) exclude a candidate with two or more null rejections in any null cell; (2) choose the highest minimum rejection rate across alternative cells; (3) break ties by the highest median log⁡E\log E in the hardest cell, the one with the lowest pooled rejection rate; (4) break remaining ties by simplicity, Kish first.

All three candidates rejected in every replicate of every alternative cell (minimum rates 100% for Kish tempering, 100% for the field mean and 100% for the site average) and in no null replicate (Kish tempering: 0/32 and 0/32 in the two null cells; the other candidates likewise, Appendix D). Step (2) therefore tied, and the selection fell to step (3). Because every cell tied on the pooled rejection rate, the “hardest cell” was not defined by the rule; the selection script took the first cell in grid order. That script was first committed together with the selection result, after the evaluation, so we cannot show that this detail was fixed in advance. In that cell the median log⁡E\log E was 131.53 for Kish tempering, 131.39 for the field mean and 83.60 for the site average. Across the twelve possible designations of the hardest cell, the rule would have selected Kish tempering in 9 of them, the field mean in 2 and the site average in 1; the Kish-minus-field-mean difference in median log⁡E\log E ranged from −-0.04 to 0.96. On this evidence Kish tempering and the field-mean score perform alike, both well ahead of the site average (Figure 2A). Kish tempering was registered for the confirmatory test; its registration describes the selection as following the pre-committed rule, and we correct that description here (Appendix D).

6.3 A pixel world model

To show the failure where machine-learning practice meets it, we ran a demonstration under a protocol frozen before any learned model was trained, with dated predictions committed before the main run. A Gaussian blob moves on an R×RR\times R frame; each action pushes it in one of four directions or leaves it, and a delayed restoring force adds memory. Frames carry independent pixel noise and one of three kinds of frame-level shared noise: none, an additive offset, or a multiplicative gain on the blob. Actions are drawn uniformly at random, so the design law is known exactly. Two learned models predict the frame four steps ahead from the last two frames and the action window, a convolutional network with action conditioning and a per-pixel ridge regression, and are compared with oracles that know the true dynamics. Each episode is one unit and its n=R2n=R^{2} pixels are its sites, from 6464 to 40964096; the effect size was calibrated on the oracle alone. Every statistic uses Monte Carlo e-values with B=127B=127 and the rejection rule E≥20E\geq 20, and reports the average of the two models.

The pooled score collapses as pixels are added, and the cause is misspecification.

Figure 1 shows the main grid. With no shared noise and the larger effect, the median log⁡E\log E of the pooled score fell from −-17.3 at 6464 pixels to −-6832 at 40964096, while the oracle’s rose from 79.0 to 157. The pattern was the same under offset and gain noise (pooled score at 40964096 pixels −-5996 and −-6567; oracle 155 and 157), and from 256256 pixels on the pooled score never rejected under any noise (0%). Because the oracle does not collapse under either form of shared noise, the collapse of the fitted models is due to their misspecification. Our protocol had predicted that the gain noise would make even the oracle collapse; it did not, because a multiplicative gain rescales the oracle’s evidence without changing its sign.

Kish tempering does not repair it here.

The pixel residuals of a misplaced blob take both signs, so their median pairwise correlation is nearly zero without shared noise or with gain noise (at most 0.000629 across cells), the Kish factor is close to one, and Kish tempering behaves like the pooled score: it rejected in 6.2% of episodes at 6464 pixels and in none from 256256 on. Under offset noise the residual correlation rose to between 0.159 and 0.182, and Kish tempering did reject, but for the wrong reason: the offset raises the residual correlation while being orthogonal to the action contrast, and at 40964096 pixels the resulting over-tempering cut its rejection rate to 43.8%. Kish tempering, the statistic registered for M5, therefore does not repair pooling amplification in the pixel world. The fractional-Kelly reference arm of §3.5, which bounds each factor below but keeps the pooled bet, rejected in 0% to 75% of episodes at the larger effect (Appendix G).

Contrast tempering restores power, not information.

Contrast tempering, declared in the protocol as an exploratory generalization, rejected in 81.2% to 100% of episodes across all noise conditions and frame sizes at the larger effect, against 100% for the oracle with the exact joint likelihood. Its median log⁡E\log E, however, stayed between 7.06 and 10.3 and did not grow with the number of pixels, far below the oracle: it removes the amplification but does not convert the additional pixels into additional evidence. At the smaller effect every learned statistic was weak (contrast tempering at most 25%).

The mechanism of §3.4 was visible directly (Figure 3). For the learned models in the main grid, the contrast design effect exceeded the Kish design effect in every row without shared noise or with gain noise (48/48) and fell below it in every offset row (24/24), as predicted before the main run. For the oracles, whose residuals are independent pixel noise, both design effects are close to one and their ordering carries no information (Appendix G).

Scope.

Every statistic was valid in every null cell. The demonstration uses one simulator family, two model classes and one training run per cell; compute limits reduced the episode length and the number of test episodes, so the intervals for alternative cells are wide (Appendix G). Contrast tempering has only this simulation evidence and no confirmatory test; it is a candidate for future registered use, not a validated method.

7 The stand-in trap

Section 2.4 and Proposition 6 describe how a predictor can make future actions look effective when they are not. The development simulations and the calibration on real command records showed the trap on biological designs (§5). Here we build it into the pixel world, where every quantity is known, and test what the randomization test needs in order to avoid it.

7.1 A pixel world with a stand-in

The logging policy now depends on state the model cannot see: with probability 0.60.6 it chooses the action that points from the blob’s position six steps earlier toward the centre of the frame, and each other action with probability 0.10.1. The model sees only the last two frames, so the future actions carry information about an earlier position that the restoring force still acts on. The actions themselves have no effect. We used 256256-pixel frames, training sets of 1616, 6464 and 256256 episodes, and either no shared noise or gain noise. The randomization test resamples each future action from the logging policy given the full logged state, which the design records.

The replacement diagnostics—retraining without actions, setting the actions to zero, and shuffling the action windows across origins within an episode—reported an action effect in most test episodes (Figure 4A): for the convolutional model in 90.6% to 100% of them, and for the ridge model in 64.1% to 100%, across diagnostics, training sizes and noise conditions. With the design-law resampler the randomization test never rejected: the Kish-tempered statistic rejected in 0% of episodes in every cell, and the contrast-tempered statistic plotted in Figure 4A in none for the two-model average (§7.2). The experiment does not show the growth of the diagnostics’ confidence with data that Proposition 6 describes: with the smallest training set, the convolutional model’s diagnostics already reported effects in at least 90.6% of episodes, leaving no room to grow. That property rests on the proposition and on the development simulations (§5.1).

7.2 The resampler must condition on the design state

The protocol included a negative control: the Kish-tempered statistic with a deliberately wrong resampler that draws each action from its marginal frequency in the training episodes, ignoring the logged state. It was expected to reject often. It never rejected (0/64 episodes in every cell), and the pre-declared criterion for the negative control was not met. The result is uninformative rather than reassuring: without shared noise or with gain noise, Kish tempering coincides with the pooled score at this frame size, and the pooled score has no power there (§6.3). A statistic whose log⁡E\log E is driven far below zero by amplification cannot reveal that a resampler is invalid.

After seeing this result we added one post hoc analysis, declared in a dated note committed before any of its e-values were computed: the same wrong resampler with the contrast-tempered statistic, which does have power, on the sealed episodes, frozen models and frozen tempering factors of the six trap cells. The wrong resampler rejected in 98.4% to 100% of episodes for the two-model average (92.2% to 100% for the individual models). With the correct resampler, whose results were read from the sealed records rather than recomputed, the same statistic never rejected for the two-model average (0/64 episodes in every cell); one single-model cell had 1/64. The wrong resampler rejected more often in 18/18 comparisons. This analysis is post hoc and exploratory; it does not replace the frozen negative control, whose criterion remains unmet.

Two lessons follow. First, the conditioning in Assumption 1 is not a technicality: a resampler that ignores part of the state the design used is far from the design law in total variation, nothing in Proposition 5 protects it, and it reproduces the false effect that the replacement diagnostics report. Second, a negative control needs a statistic with power; pooling amplification can hide invalidity as easily as it hides an effect.

7.3 Summary across settings

The same three-way pattern appears in every setting we examined. Replacement diagnostics report effects at high rates when there is none: in the development simulations, on real command records with synthetic outcomes, in the sealed challenge, and in the pixel world. A randomization test that resamples from the design law, conditioning on the full state the design used, keeps its error rate. A randomization test that resamples from a simpler law loses that guarantee and reproduces the diagnostics’ error. On the real ERK data the diagnostics reported an effect that is biologically established, so we do not count those reports as instances of the trap (§8.2).

8 Real data

The real-data evidence has three stages, each with a different evidential status. M4 is the registered analysis of two previously analyzed datasets. X is a single exploratory application of the repaired statistic to the M4 test fields. M5 is a registered confirmatory test of the repaired statistic on a field that no one involved had opened. Appendix E gives registration identifiers, hashes and the time-ordering of every data access; Appendix D lists every deviation and disclosure.

8.1 Data, units and design laws

ERK.

In the ERK experiment (Nałęcz-Jawecki et al., 2023), with data released as Nałęcz-Jawecki et al. (2022), each microscope field receives one light program, a sequence of pulses whose inter-pulse intervals were randomized by the acquisition protocol, and the field’s hundreds of cells are recorded under that common program. The field is therefore the assignment unit and its cells are sites; the spillover graph between fields is empty, so the primary null is H0GH_{0}^{G}. The working design law, V3, shuffles the inter-pulse intervals uniformly within interval groups, conditionally on the elapsed interval at the origin, and preserves the protocol’s rest segment; two variants, V1 and V2, serve as sensitivity laws. Fields run under a binary policy are deterministic and contribute e≡1e\equiv 1. The reference models were trained on four minimum-gap fields from the first replicate and tested on four minimum-gap fields from the second replicate and five ordinary-interval fields.

CcaS/CcaR.

In the CcaS/CcaR experiment (Lugagne et al., 2024), with data and trained models released as Lugagne et al. (2023), each cell lineage receives its own light program from a random walk, bounded in the released acquisition code, so each lineage is a unit with a single site. The working law, D1, is the generator in the released acquisition code delayed by one step, consistent with a shift at data export; the delay was found after the first design-law checks failed (Appendix C). Every CcaS rejection below is conditional on D1.
