Lineages that follow one of two duplicated fixed templates have zero design entropy and contribute e≡1e\equiv 1; the remaining lineages are tested under the design law conditioned on avoiding both templates (Proposition 2(b)), which keeps the test exact. In addition to the four reference models, we test the published model of Lugagne et al. (2024) with its released preprocessing, after replacing its neighbour-exposure input by the lagged, admissible version (§2.3).

Models and prior use.

The four reference models (linear-Gaussian, GRU, small Transformer and gradient boosting) are additive: an own-history branch plus an action branch fitted to its residual. They were trained on training-unit outcomes only and frozen by hash before any test outcome was opened; their Gaussian variances come from held-out validation data. Both datasets were analyzed earlier in our BioWM-Eval study (Appendix A); M4 is therefore a re-analysis, not a blind test, although every M4 setting was fixed on synthetic data and command records before the outcomes were reopened.

8.2 M4: the registered analysis

M4 tests five prespecified hypotheses with the pooled statistic (Table 2): ERK at horizons of ten and thirty minutes, registered as positive controls because optogenetic stimulation is known to drive ERK activity; CcaS at one and six five-minute steps with the four-model average; and CcaS at twelve steps with the published model. A slot is rejected iff E≥100E\geq 100, the e-Bonferroni rule for five hypotheses at family level 0.050.05.

Neither positive control was rejected, and the failure was not marginal: every reference model gave a strongly negative log⁡E\log E for ERK (from −-17,989 to −-2973), and so did both sensitivity laws. By the interpretation registered with M4, a strongly negative log⁡E\log E for a model means that its predictions under the observed actions scored worse than its predictions averaged over the design; it is not evidence against an effect. A dated note written after we had read the M4 report fixes further interpretation rules; it was written post hoc, and its rules only restrict what may be claimed (Appendix D). Section 6 shows that the failure is pooling amplification: the ERK score sums hundreds of cells that share one action sequence.

Both CcaS hypotheses at the longer horizons were rejected. Restricting the published model to lineages whose lagged exposure could be verified from commands gives log⁡E=16,771\log E=16{,}771. A second sensitivity analysis that uses the raw neighbour exposure with singleton averaging gives 3.02; it changes both the exposure alignment and the aggregation, is not a valid test, and is reported descriptively only. The secondary own-channel analysis at six steps gives log⁡E\log E from 617 to 1338 across models, but its eligibility bound is vacuous (Proposition 2(a)), so it is descriptive.

Two secondary results bear on the diagnosis. The batch randomization p-value at a single prespecified origin gave per-model values from 1/128 to 2/128 for ERK at thirty minutes and 12/128 for every model at ten minutes (unadjusted, secondary). A rank-based p-value depends only on where the observed score ranks among the design draws, not on the size of the score differences, so it does not suffer from the over-aggressive betting that drives pooling amplification. The contrast with the e-value product is consistent with the diagnosis; but the registered interface covers such p-values only at one common origin, whereas e-values combine evidence across all origins. Second, the replacement diagnostics reported an ERK action effect, with risk differences from 14.6% to 46.3%. The ERK effect is biologically real, so these are most likely true positives and we do not use them as examples of the stand-in trap. For CcaS at one step the same diagnostics reported effects of magnitude 2.9×10−82.9\times 10^{-8} to 2.9×10−42.9\times 10^{-4} while the randomization test did not reject; the truth there is unknown, so this is descriptive only.

8.3 X: an exploratory check on the M4 test fields

After diagnosing the failure (§6), we selected the Kish-tempered statistic on synthetic data and applied it once, with every parameter fixed on training data, to the nine ERK test fields of M4. We call this analysis X. It is exploratory: the fields had been opened in M4, and the analysis was run because the pooled statistic had failed there. No test outcome was used to choose the statistic or its parameters. The four-model log⁡E\log E was 349 at ten minutes and 218 at thirty minutes, against −-9576 and −-2975 for the pooled statistic on the same data; the individual models ranged from 185 to 350. The exact-form design bound of Proposition 4 for these fields is 925 at both horizons, and X reached 37.7% and 23.5% of it on the log scale. Because X used Monte Carlo e-values, this is a descriptive comparison rather than a ceiling; the corresponding Monte Carlo bound of Proposition 4(a), computed in the M5 registration package from the frozen Monte Carlo bags, is 914 at ten minutes and 848 at thirty. The ratios are not power estimates. These values are reported descriptively: X was prompted by outcomes already opened in M4, and no formal error guarantee is claimed for it.

8.4 M5: a confirmatory test on an unopened field

Design.

M5 tests the repaired statistic on one ERK field, a minimum-gap field with thirty-minute minimum intervals from the first replicate. It had been excluded from M4 by the scope of the registered sample (minimum gaps of ten to twenty-five minutes, two replicates), not for data quality. None of our projects had opened it, and before registration the first author recorded a statement that he had never opened, previewed or plotted its outcomes (Appendix E). The analysis plan was committed before X was run and was not changed afterwards (its committed and registered bytes are identical). It was registered before the data were obtained, in a new registration linked to the M4 registration, together with a disclosure that the X results were available when the plan was finalized. The only primary hypothesis is H0GH_{0}^{G} at ten minutes, rejected iff E≥20E\geq 20; thirty minutes is computed and reported descriptively only. The registered plan chose this horizon before any M5 data were obtained, because a single-field rehearsal had shown weak power at thirty minutes under shared noise (§5). The statistic is the Kish-tempered score with all parameters frozen on the training fields, the working law V3, and Monte Carlo e-values with B=127B=127.

Command-law gate.

Before any outcome statistic was computed, a registered gate checked the reconstructed command series alone: that commands were shared by all cells, that every non-rest inter-pulse interval was at least thirty minutes (the minimum was 31 minutes), that the frozen parser found the rest segment (at interval rank 15), and that the exchangeability diagnostics used for the M4 fields did not flag the interval sequence (p=0.27p=0.27, 0.370.37 and 0.560.56, against the inherited per-statistic threshold 0.01/390.01/39). The gate passed.

Result.

The primary hypothesis was rejected (Figure 5): the four-model log⁡E\log E at ten minutes was 23.1, that is E≈1.1×1010E\approx 1.1\times 10^{10}. All four models agreed (23.0, 23.0, 22.5 and 23.7). The field had 500 cells and 1581 origins; 560,409 cell–origin pairs contributed, 230,091 were excluded by the observation mask, and 1083 factors had zero design entropy. The exact-form design bound is 51.7, and the statistic reached 44.7% of it on the log scale, a descriptive comparison as for X. At thirty minutes the descriptive log⁡E\log E was 19.1 (models from 17.0 to 19.9); it carries no confirmatory decision.

What M5 shows.

Conditional on the registered design, observation-process and frozen-training assumptions, with the working law V3, the rejection is evidence against the sharp null H0GH_{0}^{G} on a new field: M5 detects the known ERK action effect with the repaired statistic. It does not estimate the size of the effect, it says nothing about power for CcaS or other systems, and it does not validate the forecast gains reported in BioWM-Eval, which answer a different question with a with-versus-without-actions comparison of the kind §7 shows can be inflated. The evidence is narrow: one field, one dataset, one horizon. The field’s thirty-minute intervals lie outside the training range of ten to twenty-five minutes, which may reduce power; the exact acquisition law for this field is unverified, so validity is conditional on V3; and the gate’s threshold, inherited from the multi-field M1 analysis, is lenient for a single field.

8.5 Kish versus contrast tempering on the ERK training fields

To ask whether the registered Kish factor is a reasonable choice on ERK, we compared it with the contrast factor of §3.4 on the training fields’ validation cells. This diagnostic is exploratory and descriptive: it used training outcomes only, computed no e-value, and touched no test field; its reading rule was fixed before the data were accessed. Expressing the contrast factor as an implied correlation ρc\rho_{c}, the pooled ratio ρc/ρ^\rho_{c}/\hat{\rho} ranged from 0.554 to 0.818 across models at ten minutes and from 0.574 to 0.828 at thirty minutes. All values fall inside the pre-declared band from 0.50.5 to 22, so by the pre-declared reading Kish tempering is approximately adequate on ERK; all are below one, so Kish tempering over-tempers somewhat and is conservative there. Individual fields gave ratios from 0.41 to 1.27; Appendix F lists every field.

Two qualifications follow from Proposition 7. Because the action branch of the ERK reference models predicts the same response for every cell of a field, the contrast is shared across cells and the contrast factor has the form of Proposition 7: a Kish factor with a contrast-weighted residual correlation, at an effective cell count since counts vary across origins. The agreement is therefore partly structural, and the diagnostic is not an independent validation of the Kish rule. And the gap is not only a matter of median versus mean: against the mean pairwise residual correlation the ratio at ten minutes was still between 0.598 and 0.854, so contrast weighting itself lowers the effective correlation; we did not decompose the remainder further. The diagnostic used the validation cells of each training field, fewer than the cells of a test field, so comparisons at test-field size assume that correlations do not change with the number of cells. We did not compute contrast-tempered e-values on the M5 field, and we make no claim about what they would have been.

9 Discussion and limitations

What to do in practice.

For anyone asking whether a world model trained on experimental data responds to actions, our results suggest five habits. First, do not read an action effect off replacement diagnostics; they answer a different question and are fooled by stand-in effects. Second, if actions were randomized, reconstruct the design law and resample from it conditionally on everything the design conditioned on; a resampler that is simpler than the design reintroduces the trap. Third, compute the design-only bound before opening any outcome; a deterministic protocol can never yield evidence, whatever the model. Fourth, when many sites share an action sequence, do not pool their log scores at face value; temper them by a design effect estimated on training data, ideally along the action contrast. Fifth, give every negative control a statistic that has power, or an invalid resampler can go unnoticed.

The confirmatory evidence is narrow.

Our only confirmatory test of the repaired statistic is one field of one dataset at one horizon. It detects an effect that biology already establishes, so it shows that the repaired test has power on real data, not that it discovers new effects; it says nothing about the size of the effect or about power in other systems. The thirty-minute horizon and the CcaS data were not part of that test.

The analysis was not blind, and part of it is post hoc.

The datasets had been analyzed before in our own earlier study, so M4 is a registered re-analysis rather than a blind test. The pooled statistic registered for M4 failed its positive controls; the diagnosis, the repair and the exploratory check X all followed that failure, and only M5 is confirmatory for the repair. The repair was selected on synthetic data under a pre-committed rule whose tie-resolution detail was implemented only after the evaluation; on this evidence the Kish-tempered and field-mean statistics are interchangeable. The sealed challenge’s designer had seen the source of the reference models. Every such departure is listed, with dates and hashes, in Appendix D.

Validity rests on assumptions about the design and the measurement.

Every guarantee is conditional on the working design law; for ERK it is a reconstruction whose exact acquisition rule is not verified for the confirmatory field, and every CcaS rejection is conditional on a one-step delay, consistent with a shift at data export, that was found after the first design checks failed. We calibrated the working laws on the released command records, but no theorem licenses them (Proposition 5). We also assume that the observation mask and segmentation do not respond to future actions. The own-channel analyses carry a vacuous eligibility bound and are descriptive only.

The repairs have limits of their own.

The tests are conservative and have little power for effects that are masked at the level of each unit or that are weak relative to the design’s entropy. Contrast tempering, the variant that restored power in the pixel world at the larger effect size, was declared before that experiment but has only simulation evidence and no confirmatory test; and even there it restored power without extracting the additional evidence that more pixels carry, so its e-values stayed far below the oracle’s. The pixel demonstration itself uses one simulator family, two model classes and one training run per cell, at reduced episode counts. Finally, a sharp-null rejection says that some site responds to some future action within the horizon; it does not say which, by how much, or through what mechanism. The authors used Claude (Claude Code and claude.ai) and Codex for code, drafting and review, and they verified all analyses and claims.

Outlook.

Three extensions would most strengthen the method: a registered confirmatory test of contrast tempering on new data; statistics that recover the evidence pooling discards rather than merely discounting it, for instance by modelling the joint error structure of the sites; and designs that are randomized with these tests in mind, since the design-only bound shows that an experiment’s evidential capacity is fixed before any model is trained. More broadly, wherever world models are evaluated on data that cannot be replayed, the experiment’s own randomization is the only source of counterfactual truth, and it is worth using.

Appendix A BioWM-Eval

Both datasets of §8 were analyzed earlier in our BioWM-Eval study. This appendix states what that study measured, how its results relate to the tests of this paper, and what its records do and do not establish about its own analysis history. The quotations and figures below are taken from the committed revision package of that study (Appendix E lists the files and hashes).

What it measured.

BioWM-Eval defined the utility of future actions as the relative reduction in the best achievable squared prediction error when the future actions are added to the state and the clock, U∗​(h)=[R0∗​(h)−R1∗​(h)]/R0∗​(h)U^{*}(h)=[R_{0}^{*}(h)-R_{1}^{*}(h)]/R_{0}^{*}(h), and estimated it by comparing held-out risks of matched fitted models with and without the future actions. In its own words, this quantity depends on the information set and does not estimate a causal effect. For ERK it compared matched one-step ridge models with and without the next programmed light pulse, both using the same past values and clock terms, and forecast thirty minutes ahead; for CcaS/CcaR it used seven leave-one-date-out comparisons at the same horizon. The ERK gain on the original minimum-gap fields was 49.6%; the CcaS gain was 0.91%, below the study’s 2% practical cutoff, which was an internal decision rule fixed before the biological analyses and not a public preregistration.

How it relates to this paper.

A with-versus-without-actions forecast comparison is the kind of diagnostic whose apparent action effects §7 shows can arise from stand-in effects. Our rejections therefore neither validate the size of the ERK gain nor say anything about whether the CcaS gain is practically meaningful: the sharp-null tests ask whether any site responds to the future actions, not how much prediction improves. Where the two studies are mentioned together, the juxtaposition is descriptive. The original ERK and CcaS/CcaR studies had already demonstrated that these systems can be predicted or controlled; BioWM-Eval did not claim those biological findings as its own, and neither do we.

What its records establish.

BioWM-Eval’s biological analyses were sequential and exploratory; unlike its synthetic challenges, none had sealed inputs or a sealed evaluator. Before the clock-controlled ERK comparison, an earlier comparison without the matched state-and-clock baseline had already been run on the same two held-out experiments, with gains of 56.2% and 57.6%. A rule-freeze record precedes the first clock-controlled result by less than an hour, but it does not name that comparison as primary, and the original project kept no version history; whether the ERK comparison was designated primary before or after its first result therefore cannot be established. The study’s synthetic challenges were sealed and revealed in a recorded order, but the challenge author and the evaluator were operated by the same agent, so its “blind” evaluations reflect an internal sealed-input order, not independent human blinding or public preregistration. These facts are why we treat M4 as a re-analysis (§8.1) and why no BioWM-Eval figure is used as evidence in this paper.

Appendix B Proofs

B.1 Sources and changes relative to the frozen documents

The obligations P1–P4 of the registered specification are proved in two theory documents that are part of the registered code archive and were therefore fixed before the registration: a core document (P1(a)–(d), P1b, P2(a)–(e), P3, P4) and a calibration supplement (P1(e) and the template-avoidance recursion). A third note in the archive covers averaging across models. Table 3 lists them with their hashes; the files used here are byte-identical to the archived ones.

The proofs below follow these documents. Writing them for the paper, we made the following changes, none of which affects the registered method: [Added] the selection, training-independence and Monte Carlo hypotheses (i)–(iii) of Proposition 1, which the frozen proofs use implicitly, together with the frozen training and design information in the conditioning fields and the grid filtration; [Tightened] the conditioning field under H0ownH_{0}^{\mathrm{own}} is written out explicitly, with the targets of units outside the independent set excluded; [Added] the hypotheses of Proposition 2(b) on the template list and on positive conditioning probability, and the derivation of the product path law from the per-origin design assumption; [Tightened] the approximate-law bound (Proposition 5), replacing a coupling argument by a direct total-variation bound conditional on the frozen baseline and defining Δ\Delta on the whole command path; [Tightened] the range of density ratios in Proposition 3 (r≥1r\geq 1, with the reversed case noted) and the conditioning on frozen training information in Proposition 4(c); [Added] for Proposition 6, the reading as independent and identically distributed copies at a fixed clock, the restriction of the frozen construction that the predictor’s window contains recent commands and constant outcomes but not the stratum, now stated in the proposition, and a written argument for its probability-one step for ideal predictors. Proposition 7 is new and is proved in §4.5.

Averages and the batch test (part (c)).

A prechosen arithmetic average of non-negative random variables with expectation at most one has expectation at most one, without any assumption on their dependence; Markov’s inequality then gives Pr⁡(E≥1/α)≤α\Pr(E\geq 1/\alpha)\leq\alpha. Averages over independent sets or models of processes adapted to the same filtration are again martingales; processes of different residue classes are adapted to different grids, and on a common clock a class factor is not conditionally mean one once part of its block is revealed, so the class average is a fixed-time e-value only. For the batch test at one common origin, the observed joint block and the joint draws are exchangeable given 𝒞t\mathcal{C}_{t} (all units under H0GH_{0}^{G}, one independent set under H0ownH_{0}^{\mathrm{own}}), and the observed-inclusive rank p-value that counts ties as exceedances is super-uniform.

B.3 Eligibility (Proposition 2)

Part (a).

Let Π∗\Pi^{*} be the pipeline that uses the structural eligibility events and Π^\hat{\Pi} the pipeline that uses command-based classifiers, run with the same statistics and Monte Carlo draws. Let DD be the event that any classifier decision differs from its structural event. On the complement of DD the two pipelines are identical. Hence, unconditionally,

Pr⁡(Π^​ rejects)≤Pr⁡(Π∗​ rejects)+Pr⁡(D)≤α+δ,\Pr(\hat{\Pi}\text{ rejects})\leq\Pr(\Pi^{*}\text{ rejects})+\Pr(D)\leq\alpha+\delta,

Index the emissions by 0,…,T−10,\dots,T-1, so that TT is the terminal clock after the last emission. The sampling transition is used only at states with positive β\beta; states with β=0\beta=0 have probability zero under the conditioned sampler.

B.4 Distributional nulls do not compose (Proposition 3)

With design law (12,12)(\tfrac{1}{2},\tfrac{1}{2}) and a score whose density ratio between the matching and the non-matching bit is rr, the exact factor is 2​r/(r+1)2r/(r+1) for a match and 2/(r+1)2/(r+1) otherwise; r=9r=9 gives 9/59/5 and 1/51/5. In system (ii), unit ii matches iff Uk=0U_{k}=0, so at each origin both units match or both fail, each with probability 12\tfrac{1}{2}. In system (i), unit 1 matches iff A1,k=UkA_{1,k}=U_{k} and unit 2 matches iff A2,k=Uk⊕A1,k⊕A2,kA_{2,k}=U_{k}\oplus A_{1,k}\oplus A_{2,k}, that is iff A1,k=UkA_{1,k}=U_{k}; again both match or both fail with probability 12\tfrac{1}{2}. The per-origin product therefore has mean 12​[(9/5)2+(1/5)2]=1.64\tfrac{1}{2}\bigl[(9/5)^{2}+(1/5)^{2}\bigr]=1.64, and the product over three independent origins has mean 1.643≈4.411.64^{3}\approx 4.41. Because (9/5)6≥20(9/5)^{6}\geq 20 while any product containing a factor 1/51/5 is below 2020, rejection at α=0.05\alpha=0.05 occurs iff both units match at all three origins, with probability 1/81/8. B.5 Design limits (Proposition 4)

Parts (a) and (b).

The exact denominator includes the term Qi,t​(Ai,tF)​eT⁡(Ai,tF)Q_{i,t}(A^{F}_{i,t})\,e^{T(A^{F}_{i,t})}, so ei,tex≤1/Qi,t​(Ai,tF)e^{\mathrm{ex}}_{i,t}\leq 1/Q_{i,t}(A^{F}_{i,t}); a point-mass law gives e≡1e\equiv 1. Within a product component, log⁡E\log E is therefore at most the sum of the corresponding per-factor log bounds. An arithmetic average of components can reach 1/α1/\alpha only if some component does. Under any alternative the actions still follow the design law, so integrating this necessary event over coherent full command paths drawn from QQ (and, for MC, over independent draws) bounds the rejection probability. Because averaging models adds no design entropy, the same command-only bound applies to the model average; for the Monte Carlo form this presumes that the models share their candidate bags, and otherwise the maximum runs over models with their own collision counts. B.7 Failure of replacement diagnostics (Proposition 6)

Positivity of the gaps.

[Added] Write Y=θ+ηY=\theta+\eta with η\eta independent centred noise of finite variance, so μ(W,F)=𝔼[θ∣W,F]\mu(W,F)=\mathbb{E}[\theta\mid W,F] and μ0​(W)=𝔼⁡[θ∣W]\mu_{0}(W)=\mathbb{E}[\theta\mid W]. As in the frozen construction, WW consists of finitely many recent commands, the recent outcomes, which are constant, and the clock, and θ\theta enters only an earlier outcome outside the window. [Tightened] This restriction is needed: if the recent outcomes revealed θ\theta, then μ⁡(W,F)=μ0​(W)=θ\mu(W,F)=\mu_{0}(W)=\theta and all three gaps would be zero. Under it, every finite command window has positive probability under both strata, because the chain is stationary with transition probabilities in (0,1)(0,1), so 0<Pr⁡(θ=1∣W)<10<\Pr(\theta=1\mid W)<1. Given the last command in WW, the first future command has stratum-specific probabilities that differ by (1−ρ)​(p1−p0)≠0(1-\rho)(p_{1}-p_{0})\neq 0, so the likelihood ratio of FF given WW between θ=1\theta=1 and θ=0\theta=0 is non-constant and μ⁡(W,⋅)\mu(W,\cdot) is non-constant on a set of windows of positive probability. (i) Hence 𝔼⁡[(μ−μ0)2]>0\mathbb{E}[(\mu-\mu_{0})^{2}]>0; if the window’s commands are removed as well, the retrained predictor is the constant Pr⁡(θ=1)\Pr(\theta=1) and the gap is Var⁡(μ)>0\mathrm{Var}(\mu)>0. (ii) Every future block, including the zero block, has positive conditional probability given WW, so μ⁡(W,0)\mu(W,0) is defined and 𝔼⁡[(μ⁡(W,F)−μ⁡(W,0))2]>0\mathbb{E}[(\mu(W,F)-\mu(W,0))^{2}]>0. (iii) With F′F^{\prime} an independent unit’s block, 𝔼⁡[(Y−μ⁡(W,F′))2]−𝔼⁡[(Y−μ⁡(W,F))2]=𝔼⁡[(μ⁡(W,F)−μ⁡(W,F′))2]>0\mathbb{E}[(Y-\mu(W,F^{\prime}))^{2}]-\mathbb{E}[(Y-\mu(W,F))^{2}]=\mathbb{E}[(\mu(W,F)-\mu(W,F^{\prime}))^{2}]>0; the cross term vanishes because 𝔼[Y−μ(W,F)∣W,F,F′]=0\mathbb{E}[Y-\mu(W,F)\mid W,F,F^{\prime}]=0 when F′F^{\prime} is independent of (Y,W,F)(Y,W,F). Under squared-error loss, each population gap equals the corresponding expected squared difference of predictors.

Probability tending to one.

[Added] For the ideal predictors the per-unit loss differences Di=(Yi−gi)2−(Yi−μi)2D_{i}=(Y_{i}-g_{i})^{2}-(Y_{i}-\mu_{i})^{2} are independent and identically distributed (over fixed pairs for the swap diagnostic), with finite variance because μ,g∈[0,1]\mu,g\in[0,1] and the noise has finite variance, and with mean equal to the population gap γ>0\gamma>0. By the law of large numbers D¯N→γ\bar{D}_{N}\to\gamma in probability, and by consistency of the nonparametric bootstrap for the mean the lower bootstrap quantile is D¯N+OP(N−1/2)\bar{D}_{N}+O_{P}(N^{-1/2}). Hence the probability that the lower interval bound exceeds zero tends to one. As in the frozen document, this is a statement about the ideal predictors. It is not claimed for fitted predictors, which would need, in addition, fitting on independent units and convergence in L2L^{2} under both the observed and the replacement input laws.

Validity of the randomization test.

The design law Q(⋅∣Ai,t,θi)Q(\cdot\mid A_{i,t},\theta_{i}) is known to the design, the outcome does not depend on any action, and the statistic uses only admissible inputs, so Proposition 1 applies: resampling from the design law preserves the dependence between the future block and θi\theta_{i}, and the size is at most α\alpha.

Two theory reviews (Appendix E) recomputed by exact enumeration the exact values stated in Propositions 3 and 4, the regression cases of the specification (exact sizes of the naive and set-averaged products under mutual spillover, shared noise and a path graph; the design ceilings for Q⁡(ON)=0.01Q(\mathrm{ON})=0.01 and for a fair bit with B=20B=20), and the forward–backward recursion and exact sampler of Proposition 2(b); the values agreed with those of the frozen documents. The first review also recomputed the exposure-clock cases. Both checked the identity of Proposition 7, which has no frozen counterpart, on random arrays. The scripts and their outputs are archived with their hashes (Table 12).

Appendix C Design laws

Every validity statement of the paper is conditional on a working design law. This appendix states each law exactly, reports how it was checked against the released command records, and lists what remains unverified. The defining documents were committed before the M4 registration; their hashes are in Appendix E.

C.1 ERK

Laws.

In each field the light program is a train of pulses whose inter-pulse intervals were randomized by the acquisition protocol. All working laws hold the first and last pulse and the leading and trailing zero-command periods at each field’s observed values. In fields with a rest of 241 minutes between pulses, the variants differ in how they treat it: V1 fixes the rest’s rank among the intervals; V2 inserts the rest after the first pulse at or beyond a threshold time taken from a stated range, sampling full arrangements uniformly by rejection; and V3, the law used for every primary analysis, shuffles the non-rest intervals before and after the rest separately. Fields without a rest reduce, under every variant, to a uniform permutation of the multiset of intervals. Counts of arrangements are counts of distinct paths, so repeated gap lengths are not double-counted. At an origin, the conditional sampler keeps the completed intervals, conditions on the time elapsed since the last pulse by rejecting a too-short ongoing gap, and returns the future pulse train. Fields run under a binary encoding policy are deterministic and contribute e≡1e\equiv 1.

Checks.

All field-by-variant combinations passed unconditional checks of multiset, rank and segment structure, and simulated combinations passed conditional checks of the future train at several origins. Before any outcome was used, each field’s observed interval sequence was compared with uniform permutations of its own non-rest multiset (10,000 permutations, fixed seed) on three statistics: the Spearman correlation of interval length with position, the number of runs up and down, and the lag-one autocorrelation of intervals. A field was to be flagged if any statistic had two-sided p<0.01/39p<0.01/39, a Bonferroni correction over thirteen fields and three statistics. No field was flagged; the smallest per-field p-value was 0.0288, and the Fisher-combined p-values were 0.2921, 0.5117 and 0.7157 for the three statistics. The same procedure gated the M5 field (§8.4).

What remains unverified.

The acquisition protocol’s finite list of interval values, the uniformity of its shuffle, the rule that triggers the rest and the treatment of the series’ edges and time budget were not established from released code. An exchangeability check cannot certify an exact randomization kernel; it can only fail to find evidence against the working law.

C.2 CcaS/CcaR

The source law.

The released acquisition code draws, for each lineage, a pair of bounds and a hidden integer that starts at the midpoint and moves up or down by one with equal probability, clipped at the bounds. For the first thirty-six steps the command is forced off while the hidden walk keeps evolving; afterwards the command is on whenever the hidden value is non-negative. The exact forward filter of this law matched an independent brute-force enumeration to rounding error.

The source law fails, and so does a fitted alternative.

Under goodness-of-fit criteria committed before any statistic was computed, which compare on- and off-run-length distributions and lag correlations of the released commands with simulations from the law, the source law was rejected: every one of the seven dates failed at least the off-run total-variation criterion. A fitted order-kk Markov model of the commands (K4) also failed the frozen gate on two dates, so no fitted kernel was admissible.

The working law D1 and when it was found.

A diagnostic recorded during that check showed that the released commands match the source law delayed by one step, consistent with a one-step shift introduced at data export. Under the delayed law (D1), the run-length total-variation distances were at most 0.01485 across dates and run types, against a frozen threshold of 0.02. The delay was not one of the candidates evaluated in advance, and its documentation does not overturn the rejection of the source law or establish the actual export transformation; D1 is therefore a working law, and every CcaS result in the paper is conditional on it. Its first numerical record is dated 2026-10-06, and the D1 implementation was committed the same day, both before the M4 registration on 2026-10-08; it was thus found after the first design-law check failed, but before any registered analysis.

Fixed templates and eligibility.

On each date, most lineages follow the random walk, but some repeat one of two fixed command templates; across dates, 2735 rows belong to 14 template groups. The templates were identified as the command paths duplicated more than ten times on a date, and frozen by hash before calibration. Template rows have zero design entropy and contribute e≡1e\equiv 1; the random-walk rows are tested under D1 conditioned on avoiding both templates of their date, computed exactly by the forward–backward recursion of Proposition 2(b). That conditioning is exact only if the templates are genuinely fixed designs; because they were inferred from released duplicates rather than released by the experimenters, this is an assumption.

Neighbour exposure.

The released neighbour-exposure covariate is aligned one step ahead of the neighbours’ commands and would let a score use other lineages’ future actions. Every CcaS score uses its lag instead (§2.3); the sensitivity analysis restricted to lineages whose lagged exposure could be verified from commands is reported in §8.2.

C.3 Status of the working laws

Proposition 5 would bound the cost of a wrong working law if the law had been fixed independently of the tested commands and its distance from the true law were known. Neither holds here: the fitted law was estimated from the released commands, and D1 was chosen after the source law failed. We therefore claim no theorem-level guarantee for the working laws and rely on calibration with the released command records (§5.2), which bounds size empirically under the commands that were actually issued.

D.3 Disclosures by stage

Before M4.

M4 is a registered re-analysis of data analyzed earlier in BioWM-Eval (Appendix A), not a blind test. During the power pilot, a documentation search incidentally displayed earlier aggregate results; no setting changed on that basis. The designer of the sealed challenge had seen the source of the reference models and one correction to the challenge design. The CcaS working law D1 was adopted after the source law failed its goodness-of-fit check, before the registration (Appendix C); every CcaS rejection is conditional on it. The own-channel eligibility bound is vacuous. Observation-process assumptions (finite masks, segmentation) are stated, not tested. Power is low for weak or masked effects, and the e-value tests are conservative. The variance floor of the published CcaS model was active. The pilot gave each synthetic ERK field one trajectory, and the end-to-end rehearsal used a simple generator; neither could reveal pooling amplification.

M4 and its aftermath.

The M4 registration was submitted, and its content fixed, before any outcome was opened. OSF’s activity log for the associated project, public since the embargoes were lifted, records its approval about two days after submission, after the M4 training and test outcomes had been accessed (Table 8); the log does not show whether the approval was given by hand or by OSF’s automatic approval, which falls due 48 hours after submission. Until approval the registration could have been cancelled; it was not, and its content is fixed by the hashes in Table 7. Neither ERK positive control was rejected in the registered analysis. The diagnosis of pooling amplification, the selection of the repair and the exploratory analysis X all followed that failure; X was run on test fields opened in M4. The dated note that fixes interpretation rules for the positive controls was written after the M4 report had been read, and its rules only restrict claims. Two operational scripts (a launcher and a report formatter) were added during the test stage and are not in the freeze manifest; their hashes are in Appendix E. M4 did not save per-field, per-factor records, so the decomposition of its log e-values by field is not available. The repaired statistic’s correlation parameter was estimated on training fields only.

M5.

The M5 registration followed X; the plan had been committed before X and was not changed afterwards, and the registration disclosed the X results. The confirmatory field’s thirty-minute intervals lie outside the ten-to-twenty-five-minute training range. The single-field rehearsal used the linear-Gaussian model only. The command-law gate inherited the multi-field threshold of M1, which is lenient for one field. Permission to retry the data download was added in the execution instruction and implemented in a separate input–output adapter; it was not used. Origins at which every cell was masked were not tallied separately. The acquisition law of the confirmatory field is unverified, so validity is conditional on V3. OSF’s activity log records the approval of the M5 registration minutes after its submission and before the first data access (Table 9); a self-reported browser visit shortly after the logged approval is also archived. Five preparation files carry modification times later than X but are byte-identical to their earlier commits.

Pixel demonstration.

All results are simulated, from one simulator family and two model classes, with one training run per cell and a reduced compute budget. Kish tempering, registered for M5, did not repair pooling amplification there; contrast tempering, which restored power at the larger effect size, is exploratory and has no confirmatory test. Two expectations of the protocol were wrong: the oracle did not collapse under gain noise, and the fitted models also collapsed under offset noise. The trap experiment could not show the diagnostics’ growing confidence with data, and its frozen negative control was uninformative; the informative negative control was added post hoc. Three dated deviation notes record a reclassified pre-freeze audit flag (blocked standard-library probes, no data access), a reconstructed counter in the negative-control code, and a refresh of version-control index metadata in another repository.

ERK training diagnostic.

Command records were copied and hashed before the access marker was created; they are design information, not outcomes. The access log merges internal hash reads into logical open events, and the new repository’s version-control identity was read from an existing repository with non-modifying commands. The agreement between the two tempering factors is partly structural (Proposition 7).

Reviews.

The theory of §4 and Appendix B was checked in two AI-assisted review sessions with read-only access to the project, distinct from the drafting sessions and from each other: the first by Claude Code, the same model family as the drafting model, and the second by Codex, a different model family. According to the project records, the frozen theory documents had themselves been written in an earlier Codex session, so neither review is independent of all the authorship involved in the way a human statistician’s would be. Every bibliography entry was checked in a separate Claude Code session, which retrieved each source and checked each attributed claim against its text. Both theory reviews recomputed the stated exact values by enumeration. Neither found an error in the frozen proofs under their stated premises, and the bibliography review found no nonexistent reference. Both theory reviews found statements in our drafts that were stronger than what had been proved; the second also found that the hypotheses added to Proposition 6 after the first review did not exclude a predictor window that reveals the stratum. The revised text narrows these statements; the review archives record each finding and how it was addressed (Table 12). The reviews check mathematics and citations; they do not certify the actual acquisition laws, the implementation of every named statistic, or the chronology of the archives.

Appendix G Pixel demonstration: full grid

The protocol, the dated predictions and every result file of the pixel demonstration are frozen and hashed (Appendix E). Compute limits fixed the episode length at the reduced level of the protocol’s pre-declared ladder, with sixteen test episodes per alternative cell, thirty-two per null cell of the main grid and sixty-four per trap cell; intervals for alternative cells are correspondingly wide. Every statistic is the average of the two learned models unless marked otherwise.

Table 16 gives the null cells of both grids: rejection counts and mean e-values for every statistic, the basis of the validity criterion. Table 18 gives the alternative cells of the main grid by noise condition, frame size and effect size: median log⁡E\log E and rejection rate for the pooled, Kish-tempered, contrast-tempered, field-mean, site-average and fractional-Kelly statistics and for the oracles. Table 21 gives the effect-report rates of the three common diagnostics in every null cell. Table 22 gives the tempering quantities of every model and cell: the median-pairwise correlation, the Kish and contrast factors and the two design effects. For the oracles, whose residuals are independent pixel noise, both design effects are close to one and their ordering is not informative; the rows in which the ordering differs from that of the learned models are all oracle rows and are marked. Table 24 gives the post hoc negative control with contrast tempering, by cell and model, next to the frozen negative control.
